## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

Table 1 ranks the enriched biological pathways associated with diabetes on the basis of statistical significance, biological coherence, and disease relevance. The overall enrichment pattern suggests that inflammation, tissue remodeling, vascular dysfunction, and endocrine intestinal biology may represent central features of diabetes. Among the strongest signals, neutrophil degranulation (REAC:R-HSA-6798695, p = 2.95 × 10−19, associated proteins = 88), complement system (WP:WP2806, p = 1.01 × 10−7, associated proteins = 25), and viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor (KEGG:04061, p = 1.20 × 10−12, associated proteins = 31) collectively indicate marked enrichment of innate immune and cytokine-linked pathways. This pattern is consistent with prior literature suggesting that chronic low-grade inflammation, neutrophil activation, and complement-mediated injury may contribute to insulin resistance, beta cell stress, and diabetic complications. In parallel, extracellular matrix organization (REAC:R-HSA-1474244, p = 4.90 × 10−14, associated proteins = 59), regulation of vasculature development (GO:1901342, p = 4.18 × 10−16, associated proteins = 50), lipid localization (GO:0010876, p = 2.83 × 10−11, associated proteins = 50), and atherosclerosis (HP:0002621, p = 4.10 × 10−2, associated proteins = 15) further support the well-established connection between diabetes, vascular injury, dyslipidemia, and extracellular matrix remodeling, processes that may underlie both microvascular disease and macrovascular disease.

Taken together, these observations extend beyond immune and vascular biology and suggest that additional metabolic and tissue-specific systems may also be involved.

In addition, the strong enrichment of small intestine; endocrine cells[High] (HPA:0481293, p = 4.12 × 10−12, associated proteins = 51), duodenum; endocrine cells[≥Low] (HPA:0151291, p = 7.62 × 10−13, associated proteins = 74), microvillus (GO:0005902, p = 4.69 × 10−3, associated proteins = 10), and carbohydrate binding (GO:0030246, p = 3.04 × 10−15, associated proteins = 33) suggests possible involvement of intestinal nutrient sensing, absorptive surface biology, and enteroendocrine signaling, all of which are increasingly recognized as regulators of glucose homeostasis and insulin secretion. Lysosome (KEGG:04142, p = 5.70 × 10−12, associated proteins = 35) and endopeptidase activity (GO:0004175, p = 3.04 × 10−15, associated proteins = 69) further point to altered proteolysis, autophagy-related degradation, and metabolic turnover, processes that have been implicated in beta cell dysfunction and diabetic tissue injury. The enrichment of factor: p53; motif: NGRCATGYCCAGRCATGYCY; match class: 1 (TF:M10023_1, p = 1.79 × 10−2, associated proteins = 38) is also notable, as p53 has been linked in prior studies to cellular stress responses, senescence, apoptosis, and metabolic dysregulation in diabetes. Finally, pathways such as axon (GO:0030424, p = 2.35 × 10−2, associated proteins = 29) and osteoarthritis (HP:0002758, p = 2.08 × 10−2, associated proteins = 14) may reflect complications and comorbid tissue damage, including diabetic neuropathy and degenerative joint changes. Overall, these highly significant enrichments support a model in which diabetes may involve not only impaired glucose regulation, but also coordinated immune activation, vascular remodeling, extracellular matrix changes, intestinal endocrine dysfunction, and stress-response signaling.

## Enriched Pathways Analysis

In the following sections, we provide a detailed discussion of the top enriched pathways.


### Factor: p53; motif: NGRCATGYCCAGRCATGYCY; match class: 1 (TF:M10023_1) 

The pathway described here centers on p53, a sequence-specific transcription factor that recognizes a characteristic deoxyribonucleic acid response element represented by the motif NGRCATGYCCAGRCATGYCY. This motif reflects the canonical p53 binding architecture, in which p53 binds as a tetramer to paired half-sites and regulates transcription of genes involved in cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis, senescence, deoxyribonucleic acid repair, and cellular stress adaptation. Through these functions, p53 acts as a major guardian of genomic integrity and a central node linking genotoxic, oxidative, metabolic, and inflammatory stress to cell fate decisions. In biological systems relevant to metabolic disease, p53 activity can influence survival and functional competence of insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells, modulate stress responses in insulin target tissues, and shape tissue remodeling under chronic nutrient excess and oxidative injury. The provided publication does not focus on diabetes pathogenesis directly, but it highlights an important mechanistic feature of this pathway: genome-editing strategies that avoid double-strand deoxyribonucleic acid breaks are less likely to trigger p53-mediated apoptosis. This observation underscores that p53 is a potent sensor of cellular stress and that excessive p53 activation can drive cell loss, a concept that is highly relevant to tissues vulnerable in diabetes, particularly pancreatic islets.  

Building on this general framework, the available publication links the p53 pathway to diabetes indirectly but meaningfully through the biology of cellular stress, genome integrity, and therapeutic engineering. The article emphasizes that base editing does not require double-strand deoxyribonucleic acid break formation and therefore is less likely to induce p53-mediated apoptosis, identifying p53 as a critical determinant of whether stressed cells survive or undergo programmed cell death. This point is relevant to diabetes because preservation of viable and functional insulin-producing cells is central to both disease prevention and treatment. In the context of diabetes, chronic metabolic stress, oxidative damage, and inflammatory burden are well-recognized drivers of beta-cell dysfunction and loss, and p53 is a major transcriptional regulator that can convert such stress signals into growth arrest or apoptosis. The publication further notes that base editing may be used to create or modify endogenous transcription factor binding sites and specifically mentions cell replacement strategies for diabetes mellitus, implying that a detailed understanding of stress-responsive transcriptional regulators such as p53 is important for safe and effective engineering of therapeutically useful cells. Thus, although the cited study does not present direct experimental evidence that altered binding of p53 to the stated motif causes diabetes, it supports a broader disease-relevant framework in which p53-dependent stress signaling influences cell survival and in which avoiding inappropriate p53 activation may improve regenerative or gene-based approaches for diabetes treatment.[PubMed:34091588](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34091588) 

Extending from the literature-based rationale to the enrichment results, a total of 553 diabetes-associated proteins were analyzed in the function enrichment analysis, and these proteins showed significant enrichment in the p53-centered transcriptional regulatory pathway defined by sequence-specific recognition of the deoxyribonucleic acid response motif NGRCATGYCCAGRCATGYCY. This pathway is biologically notable because it integrates multiple stress dimensions that are highly relevant to diabetes, including genomic injury, oxidative stress, metabolic overload, inflammatory signaling, cell-cycle control, programmed cell death, senescence, and deoxyribonucleic acid repair. From a disease perspective, the enrichment of 553 proteins indicates a broad systems-level connection between diabetes and p53-dependent stress adaptation, particularly in pancreatic beta cells and insulin-responsive tissues, where excessive stress signaling can impair cellular survival, reduce functional capacity, and promote tissue remodeling under chronic nutrient excess. The pathway description further emphasizes an important mechanistic principle, namely that genome-editing approaches that avoid double-strand deoxyribonucleic acid breaks are less likely to activate p53-driven apoptosis, supporting the interpretation that p53 functions as a quantitatively sensitive cellular stress sensor whose overactivation may contribute to cell loss in diabetes-relevant tissues.

To place this 553-protein signal into a broader systems context, the protein-protein interaction network visualization and the corresponding STRING webpage are provided below to support interpretation of the enriched network.

With this network-level overview in mind, several significant proteins identified during the function enrichment analysis may warrant closer consideration. We introduce them in detail below.

AIFM1 stands out as one of the most diabetes-relevant proteins in the list because it integrates several core processes implicated in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes: inflammatory signaling, cell death control, and stress adaptation. Its ability to inhibit caspases and modulate apoptosis is particularly important in the context of pancreatic beta-cell loss, which is central to diabetes pathogenesis. In parallel, its E3 ubiquitin ligase activity regulates nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells and nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain containing 1 or nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain containing 2 receptor-interacting serine-threonine kinase 2 signaling, linking AIFM1 to innate immune activation and chronic inflammation, both of which contribute to insulin resistance and islet dysfunction. Its influence on phosphatase and tensin homolog, mitogen-activated protein kinase pathways, and cell proliferation further suggests potential roles in insulin signaling, survival responses, and tissue remodeling under metabolic stress. Taken together, AIFM1 is mechanistically relevant to diabetes because it lies at the intersection of beta-cell viability, inflammatory injury, and metabolic stress signaling.[PubMed:11257230](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257230) [PubMed:11257231](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257231) [PubMed:11447297](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11447297) [PubMed:12121969](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12121969) [PubMed:12620238](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12620238) [PubMed:17560374](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17560374) [PubMed:17967870](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17967870) [PubMed:19473982](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19473982) [PubMed:20154138](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20154138) [PubMed:22103349](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22103349) [PubMed:19667203](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19667203) [PubMed:22607974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22607974) [PubMed:29452636](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29452636) [PubMed:30026309](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30026309) [PubMed:29020630](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29020630) [PubMed:22095281](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22095281) 

In a related but more receptor-proximal manner, CD248 is highly notable for diabetes because its annotated function directly links it to insulin signaling. Specifically, CD248 interacts with the insulin receptor and reduces its autophosphorylation in response to insulin, indicating a plausible role as a negative regulator of insulin action. This places CD248 in direct mechanistic proximity to insulin resistance, a defining feature of type 2 diabetes. In addition, CD248 promotes inflammatory cytokine production in macrophages and participates in angiogenesis and tissue remodeling, all of which are highly relevant to diabetic complications such as chronic inflammation, vascular dysfunction, and impaired tissue repair. Its combined effects on insulin responsiveness and inflammatory remodeling make CD248 a particularly compelling candidate for involvement in both metabolic dysregulation and diabetic end-organ disease.[PubMed:11489895](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11489895) [PubMed:25243742](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25243742) [PubMed:38061240](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38061240) [PubMed:30986375](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30986375) [PubMed:33830628](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33830628) [PubMed:33737161](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33737161) 

Along the same axis of metabolic inflammation, MZB1 is one of the most directly diabetes-associated entries because its functional annotation explicitly connects it to insulin resistance. As a pro-inflammatory adipokine, MZB1 may promote chronic low-grade inflammation within adipose tissue, a hallmark of obesity-associated type 2 diabetes. Its reported ability to blunt insulin responsiveness in adipocytes strongly suggests a role in impaired glucose uptake and defective insulin signaling. Because adipose tissue inflammation contributes systemically to metabolic dysfunction through cytokine release, altered lipid handling, and endocrine disruption, MZB1 may represent a mechanistic bridge between obesity, inflammation, and whole-body insulin resistance. This makes it especially relevant to the early pathogenesis and progression of type 2 diabetes.

Shifting from adipose inflammation toward immune regulation and organ-specific injury, HAVCR1 is particularly relevant to diabetes because it combines immunoregulatory and renal repair functions. Its role in regulatory B-cell homeostasis and induction of anti-inflammatory mediators such as interleukin 10 suggests that it may influence immune tolerance and inflammatory balance, which are central to autoimmune beta-cell destruction in type 1 diabetes and to chronic inflammation in type 2 diabetes. Equally important, HAVCR1 is implicated in kidney injury and repair, making it highly relevant to diabetic kidney disease, one of the most common and serious complications of diabetes. Thus, HAVCR1 may connect systemic immune dysregulation with tissue-specific injury responses in the diabetic kidney.[PubMed:21821911](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21821911) [PubMed:25645598](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25645598) [PubMed:32668241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32668241) [PubMed:24703780](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24703780) [PubMed:25582854](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25582854) [PubMed:15793576](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15793576) 

From immune balance, the discussion then moves toward post-transcriptional control of growth factor signaling. GIGYF2 is relevant to diabetes because it is linked to post-transcriptional gene regulation and, importantly, to insulin and insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor signaling through cooperation with growth factor receptor-bound protein 10. Growth factor receptor-bound protein 10 is a well-established modulator of insulin receptor activity, and therefore GIGYF2 may influence insulin sensitivity by shaping receptor-proximal signaling output. In addition, its role in translational repression and ribosome-associated quality control suggests that it could affect cellular adaptation to nutrient excess, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and proteostasis imbalance, all of which are prominent in metabolic disease. GIGYF2 therefore stands out as a regulator with plausible effects on insulin action and stress responses in metabolically active tissues.[PubMed:26763119](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26763119) [PubMed:12771153](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12771153) 

Continuing with insulin signaling, PIK3IP1 is highly pertinent to diabetes because the phosphoinositide 3-kinase pathway is a central mediator of insulin signaling in liver, muscle, and adipose tissue. As a negative regulator of hepatic phosphoinositide 3-kinase activity, PIK3IP1 could attenuate insulin-mediated suppression of gluconeogenesis and other anabolic responses in the liver, thereby contributing to hyperglycemia and hepatic insulin resistance. Given that excessive hepatic glucose production is a major driver of fasting hyperglycemia in type 2 diabetes, proteins that constrain phosphoinositide 3-kinase signaling are of substantial mechanistic interest. PIK3IP1 therefore represents a plausible molecular brake on insulin action in the liver.

A related metabolic layer involves vascular and endothelial homeostasis. ASS1 is relevant to diabetes because arginine metabolism is closely linked to nitric oxide production, endothelial function, and metabolic homeostasis. In diabetes, impaired arginine availability and altered nitric oxide biology contribute to endothelial dysfunction, vascular complications, and abnormalities in insulin action. As a key enzyme in arginine biosynthesis, ASS1 may influence substrate availability for nitric oxide synthase and thereby affect vascular tone and tissue perfusion. This is particularly important in diabetic complications involving the microvasculature, including nephropathy, retinopathy, and impaired wound healing. Although not a classical diabetes gene, ASS1 is mechanistically connected to metabolic and vascular dysfunction in diabetes.

Closely aligned with this vascular theme, CBS is of interest in diabetes because it regulates homocysteine disposal and hydrogen sulfide generation, both of which have implications for vascular and metabolic health. Elevated homocysteine is associated with endothelial dysfunction and cardiovascular risk, which are major concerns in diabetes. Meanwhile, hydrogen sulfide has cytoprotective and signaling properties that may influence oxidative stress responses, vascular relaxation, and possibly beta-cell physiology. Through these functions, CBS may affect the redox and vascular environment that shapes diabetic complications, especially those involving the cardiovascular system and microcirculation.

From vascular redox balance, the discussion naturally extends to antioxidant defense. TXNRD1 is strongly relevant to diabetes because oxidative stress is a major pathogenic driver of insulin resistance, beta-cell dysfunction, and diabetic complications. By maintaining thioredoxin in its reduced state and detoxifying reactive oxygen species such as hydrogen peroxide, TXNRD1 supports cellular antioxidant defenses. This is especially important in pancreatic beta cells, which are relatively vulnerable to oxidative injury, and in vascular tissues exposed to chronic hyperglycemia. Impairment or dysregulation of redox control systems can exacerbate glucotoxicity, inflammation, and endothelial damage. Accordingly, TXNRD1 represents an important protective node in the cellular response to metabolic stress.

Another stress-responsive process of interest is endoplasmic reticulum proteostasis. ENTPD5 is relevant to diabetes because endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis and glycoprotein folding are critical for secretory cells, particularly pancreatic beta cells, which synthesize and process large amounts of insulin. By clearing uridine diphosphate from the endoplasmic reticulum lumen and promoting uridine diphosphate glucose regeneration, ENTPD5 supports protein reglucosylation and quality control. This function may help preserve proper folding of secretory and membrane proteins under conditions of metabolic stress. Since endoplasmic reticulum stress is a well-established contributor to beta-cell dysfunction and insulin resistance, ENTPD5 may influence diabetes susceptibility or progression through its effects on proteostasis.[PubMed:10369669](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10369669) [PubMed:21074248](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21074248) 

This emphasis on beta-cell function leads naturally to transcriptional regulation in key metabolic organs. PCBD1 is particularly noteworthy because its annotation explicitly highlights a role in pancreatic islet cells and liver, the two organs most central to glucose homeostasis. As a transcriptional activator, PCBD1 may contribute to cell-type-specific gene expression programs that support endocrine pancreatic function and hepatic metabolism. Dysregulation of transcriptional networks in islets can impair insulin production or secretion, while altered liver gene expression contributes to abnormal glucose output and lipid metabolism. Therefore, PCBD1 is a plausible regulator of diabetes-relevant transcriptional programs, even if its exact role in disease requires further clarification.[PubMed:19289501](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19289501) [PubMed:10966642](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10966642) [PubMed:30555544](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30555544) 

Staying within the endocrine pancreas, FAM3B is one of the clearest diabetes-relevant proteins in the dataset because it directly induces apoptosis of pancreatic alpha and beta cells. Beta-cell loss is a defining lesion in both type 1 diabetes and advanced type 2 diabetes, while alpha-cell dysfunction contributes to dysregulated glucagon secretion and worsening hyperglycemia. A factor capable of promoting death in both endocrine cell populations could therefore have profound consequences for islet integrity and glycemic control. FAM3B is especially important because it connects islet cell survival directly to diabetes pathophysiology rather than indirectly through systemic inflammation or vascular injury.

Beyond endocrine cell survival, lysosomal and nutrient-sensing pathways may also contribute to metabolic vulnerability. NAGPA is relevant to diabetes because lysosomal trafficking and nutrient-sensitive glycosylation pathways are increasingly recognized as important in metabolic homeostasis. Proper mannose 6-phosphate tagging is required for lysosomal enzyme delivery, and lysosomal dysfunction can impair autophagy, organelle quality control, and insulin-responsive metabolism. In addition, hydrolysis of uridine diphosphate N-acetylglucosamine links NAGPA to hexosamine-related glycosylation pathways, which are responsive to nutrient excess and implicated in insulin resistance. Therefore, NAGPA may have indirect but meaningful relevance to diabetes through lysosomal function and metabolic signaling.

A parallel metabolic vulnerability involves iron handling. HEPH is relevant to diabetes because iron overload and altered iron handling are associated with insulin resistance, beta-cell toxicity, and increased risk of type 2 diabetes. By facilitating iron efflux and transfer to transferrin, HEPH contributes to systemic iron balance. Disturbances in this process may promote oxidative stress and metabolic dysfunction, particularly in liver and pancreas, where excess iron can impair insulin signaling and secretory capacity. Thus, HEPH is important as a regulator of a metabolic cofactor that can become pathogenic when dysregulated in diabetes.[PubMed:22961397](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22961397) [PubMed:37277838](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37277838) 

Consistent with this theme, SCARA5 is notable in the diabetes context because it regulates cellular iron uptake independently of transferrin. Iron metabolism has strong relevance to diabetes, as excessive intracellular iron can drive oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired insulin action. Because ferritin-mediated iron delivery may operate in specific tissues and developmental contexts, SCARA5 could influence tissue-specific iron loading and susceptibility to metabolic injury. Its role is especially relevant to organs vulnerable in diabetes, such as kidney, liver, and pancreas, where altered iron handling may exacerbate disease progression.

From iron metabolism, attention can shift to coordinated control of cell growth and inflammatory activation. LATS1 is mechanistically important for diabetes because it connects growth control, apoptosis, and innate inflammatory signaling. Hippo-yes-associated protein signaling has recognized roles in beta-cell proliferation, regeneration, and survival, making LATS1 a potentially important regulator of islet mass. In addition, the recently annotated ability of LATS1 to promote NLR family pyrin domain containing 3 inflammasome activation is highly relevant, since NLR family pyrin domain containing 3-driven inflammation contributes to insulin resistance, beta-cell stress, and diabetic complications. Therefore, LATS1 may influence diabetes through both tissue remodeling and inflammatory mechanisms.[PubMed:10518011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10518011) [PubMed:10831611](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10831611) [PubMed:18158288](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18158288) [PubMed:26437443](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26437443) [PubMed:28068668](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28068668) [PubMed:15122335](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15122335) [PubMed:19927127](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19927127) [PubMed:9988268](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9988268) [PubMed:15220930](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15220930) [PubMed:39173637](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39173637) 

This brings the discussion to vascular integrity, a recurring theme across diabetic complications. GDF2 is highly relevant to diabetes because vascular dysfunction is a central feature of both microvascular and macrovascular diabetic complications. GDF2 helps maintain vascular integrity, regulate endothelial migration, and coordinate signaling through SMAD pathways in endothelial cells. Such functions are directly pertinent to diabetic retinopathy, nephropathy, impaired wound healing, and broader endothelial dysfunction associated with chronic hyperglycemia. By influencing endothelial stability and remodeling, GDF2 may affect susceptibility to vascular injury in diabetes.[PubMed:10625534](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10625534) [PubMed:17540773](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17540773) [PubMed:28530658](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28530658) [PubMed:23300529](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23300529) 

In the same vascular context, vascular endothelial growth factor A-related signaling is among the most established pathways in diabetic complications, particularly diabetic retinopathy and nephropathy, where pathological angiogenesis and vascular permeability are key pathogenic events. The annotated functions include endothelial proliferation, migration, permeability control, and nitric oxide production, all of which are highly relevant to diabetic microvascular disease. Aberrant activation of this pathway can drive leaky and proliferative vasculature, whereas insufficient signaling can impair tissue repair. Therefore, this protein stands out as a major mediator of diabetes-associated vascular pathology.[PubMed:10377427](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10377427) [PubMed:17951249](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17951249) 

A related but more indirect aspect of tissue adaptation involves hypoxia and acid-base regulation. CA9 may have relevance to diabetes through regulation of pH homeostasis and tissue adaptation to hypoxia and metabolic stress. Diabetic tissues often experience altered metabolism, local hypoxia, and acid-base disturbances, especially in poorly perfused organs and in the tumor-like microenvironments of chronically inflamed tissue. Carbonic anhydrase activity can shape extracellular acidity, cellular metabolism, and survival under stress conditions. Although the diabetes connection is indirect, CA9 may be relevant in the context of diabetic tissue remodeling and hypoxic injury.

From tissue stress, the focus then narrows to renal and urinary tract defense. UMOD is particularly relevant to diabetes because urinary tract infection and kidney injury are common in diabetic patients. Its ability to bind type 1 fimbriated *Escherichia coli* and promote bacterial clearance suggests a protective role in urinary tract defense, which is clinically important given the increased susceptibility to infection in diabetes. In addition, its contribution to urinary physicochemical homeostasis may be relevant to diabetic kidney stress. UMOD therefore stands out more as a modifier of diabetic renal and urinary complications than as a driver of glycemic dysregulation itself.[PubMed:14871399](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14871399) [PubMed:15327412](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15327412) [PubMed:11134021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11134021) 

Another mechanism relevant to chronic hyperglycemia involves handling of glycated macromolecules and matrix turnover. STAB2 has a meaningful connection to diabetes because it binds and clears advanced glycation end products, which accumulate during chronic hyperglycemia and contribute to vascular injury, inflammation, and tissue stiffness. Its role in extracellular matrix turnover and apoptotic cell clearance further links it to chronic inflammatory remodeling, a process central to diabetic vasculopathy and organ damage. By influencing advanced glycation end product handling and tissue homeostasis, STAB2 may modulate the severity of diabetic complications, especially in the vasculature and liver.

Lipid trafficking provides an additional layer of metabolic relevance. NPC2 is relevant to diabetes because cholesterol trafficking and lysosomal lipid handling are tightly linked to insulin sensitivity, hepatic metabolism, and lipotoxicity. Dysregulated intracellular cholesterol distribution can impair membrane composition, organelle function, and inflammatory signaling. In metabolically active tissues such as liver and macrophages, these processes contribute to steatosis, inflammation, and insulin resistance. NPC2 therefore represents a lipid-handling protein with plausible importance in the metabolic context of type 2 diabetes.[PubMed:12591949](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12591949) [PubMed:17018531](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17018531) [PubMed:21315718](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21315718) [PubMed:26296895](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26296895) 

Finally, extending this metabolic perspective to biosynthetic and inflammatory pathways, MVK is potentially relevant to diabetes because the mevalonate pathway contributes to cholesterol synthesis, prenylation reactions, and inflammatory signaling. Alterations in lipid biosynthesis and prenylation can affect insulin signaling, mitochondrial function, and immune activation. Given the strong relationship between dyslipidemia and type 2 diabetes, enzymes in the mevalonate pathway such as MVK may influence metabolic disease susceptibility and progression, particularly in the liver.[PubMed:11278915](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11278915) [PubMed:18302342](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18302342) [PubMed:9325256](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9325256) [PubMed:9392419](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9392419)

### microvillus (GO:0005902) 

Microvilli are thin, actin filament-supported, membrane-covered projections that densely populate the apical surface of absorptive epithelial cells, especially in the small intestine, where they collectively form the brush border. Their principal biological role is to expand apical membrane area and thereby optimize nutrient, ion, water, and metal absorption, while also organizing digestive enzymes and transporter complexes within a specialized membrane environment. Beyond simple surface amplification, microvilli function as dynamic structural and signaling platforms whose composition depends on membrane lipids, cytoskeletal linkers, scaffolding proteins, and regulated trafficking of transporters to and from the brush border. In the context of diabetes, the publications provided suggest that the diabetic state alters several key properties of this compartment, including membrane lipid composition and fluidity, localization of transport proteins, and assembly of transporter-associated regulatory complexes. In experimental diabetes, intestinal microvillus membranes show increased cholesterol content and reduced membrane fluidity, together with altered brush border enzyme activities, indicating that diabetes remodels the physical and functional state of the absorptive surface itself. In parallel, diabetes changes the abundance and apical targeting of major transport systems within the brush border, suggesting that microvilli may act not merely as passive structures, but as central effectors of epithelial dysfunction and adaptation in metabolic disease.  

Building on this general framework, the collected studies support a clear link between microvillus biology and diabetes by showing that diabetes remodels the intestinal brush border at structural, biophysical, and transporter-regulatory levels, with important consequences for fluid balance, nutrient handling, and metal absorption. The strongest mechanistic evidence comes from work showing that streptozotocin-induced diabetes reduces the brush border membrane expression and activity of sodium hydrogen exchanger three together with associated scaffolding and cytoskeletal regulators, including sodium hydrogen exchanger regulatory factor one, inositol trisphosphate receptor-binding protein released with inositol trisphosphate, and ezrin; this disrupts macrocomplex formation at the apical surface, impairs fluid absorption, and contributes to diabetic diarrhea, whereas insulin restores complex assembly, brush border localization, and transport function, and lysophosphatidic acid can also rescue this pathway through an insulin-independent mechanism (PubMed:26258413). Complementing this, an earlier study demonstrated that chronic experimental diabetes decreases ileal microvillus membrane fluidity because of increased cholesterol and an elevated cholesterol-to-phospholipid ratio, with insulin correcting these membrane lipid abnormalities, indicating that the diabetic state alters the physicochemical environment in which brush border transporters and enzymes operate (PubMed:3900076). Diabetes also promotes abnormal apical enrichment of the iron transporter divalent metal transporter one: in diabetic mice and in intestinal samples from patients with diabetes, brush border expression increases disproportionately relative to total protein abundance, and high glucose drives this redistribution through protein kinase C alpha-dependent stabilization and reduced internalization, thereby enhancing intestinal iron uptake and potentially contributing to diabetic iron loading, a process relevant because excess iron can aggravate metabolic dysfunction and complications (PubMed:30423260). Additional studies further suggest that diabetes-associated remodeling of brush border and villus function extends to altered sodium-glucose transport, sodium chloride absorption, and developmental programming of intestinal transport and enzyme systems in offspring exposed to gestational diabetes, reinforcing the concept that the microvillus compartment is a major intestinal target of diabetic dysregulation rather than a merely incidental structure (PubMed:31107610, PubMed:21964563). Finally, studies of metabolic adaptation after bariatric procedures and microbiota-driven intestinal remodeling show that changes in villus and microvillus architecture are closely linked to systemic insulin sensitivity and glycemic improvement, supporting the broader idea that microvillus structure and function participate in whole-body metabolic homeostasis and may influence diabetic phenotypes even when not the primary initiating lesion. Taken together, the available evidence indicates that diabetes alters microvillus membrane composition, transporter trafficking, and absorptive signaling complexes, and that these changes contribute to clinically relevant intestinal manifestations of diabetes while also intersecting with systemic metabolic control.[PubMed:26258413](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26258413) [PubMed:3900076](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3900076) [PubMed:30423260](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30423260) [PubMed:31107610](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31107610) [PubMed:21964563](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21964563) [PubMed:39410706](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39410706) [PubMed:26638070](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26638070) [PubMed:26185767](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26185767) 

With this literature context in place, the pathway enrichment result can be interpreted more coherently in relation to the observed diabetes-associated signal. There were 10 diabetes-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing microvilli as thin, actin filament-supported, membrane-covered projections that densely populate the apical surface of absorptive epithelial cells, especially in the small intestine, where they collectively form the brush border. This enrichment is biologically notable because the pathway centers on a highly specialized absorptive membrane domain that regulates nutrient, ion, water, and metal uptake, and the available evidence indicates that diabetes alters this compartment at multiple levels, including membrane lipid composition, membrane fluidity, brush border enzyme activity, transporter abundance, and apical transporter targeting. In this context, the identification of 10 proteins supports a focused but potentially functionally coherent disease signal, consistent with the concept that diabetes remodels the physical and regulatory architecture of the absorptive epithelial surface rather than affecting a single isolated transport event. The pathway description further indicates that diabetes is associated with increased cholesterol content and reduced membrane fluidity in intestinal microvillus membranes, together with altered assembly of transporter-associated regulatory complexes, providing mechanistic support for why proteins enriched in this microvillus-related pathway may contribute to epithelial dysfunction and adaptive responses in metabolic disease.

To further contextualize these findings, the interaction network offers a useful view of how the 10 enriched proteins may relate to one another at the systems level. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 10 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here: [Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=92DCDAFB6BD5D2C9).

![PPI Network](imgs/52f7da95-116b-46f9-8966-3b504496df20.png)

Having outlined the network-level result, the individual proteins can now be introduced in a more detailed and connected manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  
AOC3 stands out as one of the most diabetes-relevant proteins in this list because its dual enzymatic and adhesion functions intersect with two central components of diabetic pathology: oxidative stress and vascular inflammation. Its oxidative deamination reaction produces hydrogen peroxide, a reactive oxygen species that can contribute to endothelial dysfunction, a hallmark of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes and a major driver of microvascular and macrovascular complications. Equally important, AOC3 promotes lymphocyte adhesion and extravasation at the endothelial surface, linking it to chronic low-grade inflammation, which is now recognized as a key mechanism in insulin resistance, adipose tissue dysfunction, and diabetic vascular injury. Through these combined roles, AOC3 may contribute to inflammatory leukocyte recruitment and oxidative damage within the vasculature, thereby plausibly influencing diabetic complications such as retinopathy, nephropathy, and atherosclerotic disease.  

In a related but distinct way, CBLIF appears relevant because it connects epithelial absorption with nutrient-dependent complications that are frequently encountered in diabetes. CBLIF is highly relevant to diabetes because it links intestinal nutrient absorption, renal tubular handling, and vitamin B12 metabolism. The most direct diabetes connection is its role in cobalamin uptake, since vitamin B12 deficiency is common in patients with type 2 diabetes receiving metformin therapy. Impaired B12 homeostasis can worsen peripheral neuropathy or confound the evaluation of diabetic neuropathy, making proteins involved in cobalamin transport particularly important in the diabetic setting. In addition, CBLIF participates in the uptake of lipoproteins and other circulating proteins in absorptive epithelia, suggesting broader relevance to metabolic homeostasis and renal function. Its expression in renal proximal tubules is also notable because tubular protein handling is frequently altered in diabetic kidney disease. Thus, CBLIF is important not because it is a classical glucose-regulatory protein, but because it lies at the interface of nutrient absorption, metabolic regulation, and renal epithelial function, all of which are clinically significant in diabetes.[PubMed:10371504](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10371504) [PubMed:11606717](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11606717) [PubMed:11717447](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11717447) [PubMed:14576052](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14576052) [PubMed:9572993](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9572993) 

Extending this absorptive and metabolic perspective, ENPP7 may be of interest because it connects intestinal lipid processing with pathways implicated in insulin resistance. ENPP7 is particularly interesting in the context of diabetes because it directly affects intestinal lipid handling and ceramide generation, both of which are mechanistically relevant to insulin resistance and cardiometabolic disease. Ceramides are now widely implicated in metabolic dysfunction, including impaired insulin signaling, lipotoxicity, hepatic steatosis, and inflammation. By hydrolyzing sphingomyelin and influencing ceramide production in the gastrointestinal tract, ENPP7 may modulate the intestinal contribution to systemic lipid metabolism. Its additional role in fatty acid absorption and its potential effect on cholesterol absorption further strengthen its relevance to the dyslipidemia that commonly accompanies type 2 diabetes. Moreover, its ability to inactivate platelet-activating factor suggests a possible anti-inflammatory dimension, which may also be meaningful given the inflammatory basis of metabolic disease. Overall, ENPP7 is notable because it connects gut lipid digestion with ceramide biology, two pathways that are increasingly recognized as contributors to insulin resistance and diabetic metabolic complications.[PubMed:12671034](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12671034) [PubMed:12885774](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12885774) [PubMed:15205117](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15205117) [PubMed:16255717](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16255717) [PubMed:28292932](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28292932) 

Shifting from epithelial metabolism to vascular regulation, TEK may represent another biologically plausible point of intersection with diabetes-related pathology. TEK is among the most compelling proteins in relation to diabetes because vascular dysfunction is a defining feature of diabetic complications. The TEK/TIE2 axis is central to endothelial stability, angiogenic remodeling, and maintenance of intercellular junctions. These processes are highly relevant to diabetic retinopathy, nephropathy, impaired wound healing, and broader microvascular injury, all of which involve endothelial destabilization, abnormal angiogenesis, and increased vascular permeability. The fact that TEK regulates endothelial cell contact integrity and VE-cadherin adhesive function is especially important, as barrier dysfunction contributes to tissue edema, inflammatory cell infiltration, and progressive organ damage in diabetes. Its role in blood vessel remodeling further suggests relevance to the pathological neovascularization observed in advanced diabetic retinopathy. Therefore, TEK stands out as a vascular homeostasis regulator whose dysfunction or altered signaling could plausibly participate in the progression of diabetic vascular disease.[PubMed:26773517](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26773517) 

Returning to the structural organization of the brush border itself, CDHR5 may be relevant through its contribution to epithelial polarity and apical membrane integrity. CDHR5 has a more indirect but still potentially meaningful connection to diabetes through its role in epithelial brush border organization. Proper microvillar architecture is essential for nutrient absorption in the intestine and for specialized epithelial function in other tissues. Because diabetes is closely linked to altered nutrient handling, intestinal metabolism, and epithelial barrier abnormalities, proteins that maintain brush border structure may influence metabolic homeostasis at the tissue level. In addition, epithelial polarity and apical membrane organization are important in renal tubular physiology, which is highly relevant to diabetic kidney disease. Although CDHR5 is not a canonical diabetes gene, its function in maintaining microvillar organization makes it a plausible modifier of absorptive or epithelial processes that can become dysregulated in metabolic disease.  

Closely aligned with this theme, CDHR2 may also warrant consideration as part of epithelial programs that shape nutrient processing and tissue homeostasis. CDHR2 is less directly connected to diabetes than AOC3, ENPP7, CBLIF, or TEK, but it remains of interest because of its role in organizing epithelial microvilli. In metabolic disease, epithelial surface specialization can influence nutrient absorption and tissue homeostasis, particularly in the intestine. Altered absorptive function may contribute to systemic metabolic imbalance, including obesity and insulin resistance, which are major drivers of type 2 diabetes. Its broader role as a structural organizer also suggests that disruption of epithelial architecture could modify tissue responses to chronic hyperglycemia or inflammation. While the evidence for a direct diabetes link is limited in the present annotation, CDHR2 may still be relevant as part of epithelial programs that influence nutrient processing and barrier function.[PubMed:19447093](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19447093) [PubMed:24725409](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24725409) [PubMed:26812018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26812018)

### axon (GO:0030424) 

The axon is the elongated neuronal projection specialized for the propagation of electrical impulses from the cell body toward presynaptic terminals, where neurotransmitters are released to communicate with target cells. Its structure and function depend on highly coordinated membrane excitability, cytoskeletal organization, mitochondrial energy production, calcium homeostasis, axonal transport, and interactions with myelinating glial cells and immune cells. Distinct subdomains of the axon, including the axon initial segment and nodes of Ranvier, regulate action potential initiation and saltatory conduction, whereas distal sensory axons and intraepidermal nerve fibers are especially vulnerable to metabolic stress because of their length and high energetic demand. In disease states, axons can exhibit early functional impairment before overt degeneration, including altered excitability, reduced neurogenic vasodilatation, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired transport of messenger ribonucleic acids and proteins, axonal swelling, failure of regeneration, and eventual loss of terminal fibers. Thus, the axon is not merely a passive cable, but a dynamic metabolic and signaling compartment whose integrity is essential for peripheral sensation, autonomic regulation, and central nervous system function.  

Against this biological background, the collected literature suggests that axonal biology is deeply implicated in diabetes, particularly in diabetic peripheral neuropathy, but also in central nervous system dysfunction and possibly in pancreatic and renal complications. In peripheral nerves, diabetes and prediabetic metabolic stress appear to produce early axonal dysfunction before frank fiber loss, as shown by impaired axonal mitochondrial membrane potential, reduced energetic reserve, altered intra-axonal calcium, and defective impulse conduction in sensory axons exposed to high dietary fat, supporting the concept that dyslipidemia-driven bioenergetic failure may be an initiating event in neuropathy (PubMed:33785643). Consistently, reduced axon reflex-mediated neurogenic vasodilatation and histamine-induced flare responses in people with diabetes provide functional evidence for early small-fiber axonal dysfunction and suggest that cutaneous sensory axons may be compromised even before advanced neuropathy is established (PubMed:22529938, PubMed:35121142, PubMed:39692076, PubMed:37382347). Morphological studies further suggest that axonal injury begins early, because axonal swellings are associated with type two diabetes even when intraepidermal nerve fiber density remains relatively preserved, indicating subclinical sensory axon stress (PubMed:33483760). Mechanistically, several studies identify possible drivers of axonal degeneration and failed repair in diabetes: hyperglycemia enhances sirtuin three-dependent deacetylation of sterile alpha and Toll interleukin receptor motif-containing protein one, increasing nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide cleavage, oxidative stress, adenosine triphosphate depletion, and sensory axon loss, whereas preserving acetylation appears protective (PubMed:41512034); impaired nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide metabolism is further supported by the finding that nicotinamide mononucleotide and nicotinamide riboside restore mitochondrial function and prevent experimental diabetic neuropathy (PubMed:35563288). Diabetes also appears to suppress regenerative competence through p35-mediated cyclin-dependent kinase five hyperactivity, glycogen synthase kinase three beta activation, and inhibitory phosphorylation of collapsin response mediator protein two, thereby blocking axon regrowth after injury in both type one and type two diabetic models (PubMed:41296830). Human nerve transcriptomic analysis similarly shows inflammatory remodeling together with neuronal transcript changes consistent with disturbed messenger ribonucleic acid localization in distal sensory axons, suggesting that altered axonal maintenance programs may contribute to degeneration in diabetic peripheral neuropathy (PubMed:40828619). Importantly, axonal injury in diabetes may not be purely cell autonomous: infiltrating C-C motif chemokine receptor two-positive macrophages in obese prediabetic mice delay terminal sensory axon degeneration through galectin three, indicating that immune responses can transiently protect axons during early neuropathy (PubMed:39939762). Beyond the peripheral nervous system, type two diabetes is associated with shortening of the axon initial segment in the medial prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, a structural change expected to reduce neuronal excitability and potentially contribute to cognitive and mood impairment; methylglyoxal, a diabetes-associated reactive metabolite, appears sufficient to induce this axon initial segment shortening and disrupt neuronal network activity (PubMed:29937715, PubMed:34531281). Additional work links diabetes to altered sensory axonal excitability and potassium channel-related properties in painful neuropathy (PubMed:41319475), while pancreatic imaging studies identify neuronal axons among the tissue features most informative for distinguishing type two diabetes, implying that axonal remodeling may extend to the endocrine pancreas (PubMed:41663377). Finally, the relevance of axon-related signaling may extend beyond neuropathy, as circulating axon guidance pathway proteins are associated with progression of diabetic kidney disease to end-stage kidney disease (PubMed:34140396). Taken together, these studies support a unifying view in which diabetes disrupts axonal metabolism, excitability, structural integrity, transport, and regenerative capacity across multiple tissues, making the axon a central pathological target and a promising therapeutic focus in diabetes.[PubMed:39939762](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39939762) [PubMed:41663377](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41663377) [PubMed:33785643](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33785643) [PubMed:29937715](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29937715) [PubMed:41296830](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41296830) [PubMed:40828619](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40828619) [PubMed:41512034](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41512034) [PubMed:34140396](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34140396) [PubMed:22529938](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22529938) [PubMed:33483760](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33483760) [PubMed:41319475](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41319475) [PubMed:39692076](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39692076) [PubMed:35121142](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35121142) [PubMed:37382347](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37382347) [PubMed:35563288](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35563288) [PubMed:34531281](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34531281) 

Building on this literature context, the enrichment result provides a complementary molecular view of the same theme. There were 29 diabetes-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing the axon as the elongated neuronal projection specialized for the propagation of electrical impulses from the cell body toward presynaptic terminals, where neurotransmitters are released to communicate with target cells. This enrichment highlights a functionally coherent set of proteins linked to membrane excitability, cytoskeletal organization, mitochondrial energy production, calcium homeostasis, axonal transport, myelinating glial cell interactions, and immune cell interactions, all of which are central to axonal integrity and are highly relevant to diabetes-associated neural dysfunction. Given that the analyzed set contains 29 proteins, the enrichment signal supports a substantial convergence of diabetes-related molecular changes on axonal biology, particularly in compartments with high metabolic demand such as the axon initial segment, nodes of Ranvier, distal sensory axons, and intraepidermal nerve fibers. These observations are consistent with the view that, in diabetes, axonal dysfunction can precede overt degeneration and may involve altered excitability, reduced neurogenic vasodilatation, mitochondrial impairment, defective transport of messenger ribonucleic acids and proteins, axonal swelling, regenerative failure, and eventual terminal fiber loss.

To further contextualize these 29 enriched proteins, the network representation below provides an overview of their protein-protein interaction structure and allows visual inspection of their connectivity.

The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for the 29 enriched proteins, together with the link to the STRING webpage for interactive inspection of the same network.

With this network-level view in place, the following paragraphs introduce several of the significant proteins identified in the enrichment analysis and discuss their possible relevance to diabetes in a cautious and data-guided manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

ALDH1A1 is among the most diabetes-relevant proteins in this list because it intersects directly with several core pathogenic mechanisms of diabetes and its complications. First, its ability to detoxify lipid peroxidation-derived aldehydes is highly pertinent to diabetes, a condition characterized by chronic oxidative stress and accumulation of reactive carbonyl species. Such aldehydes can damage proteins, lipids, and cellular membranes, thereby contributing to beta-cell dysfunction, insulin resistance, and tissue injury in the retina, kidney, vasculature, and lens. Second, ALDH1A1 is linked to the metabolism of 3-deoxyglucosone, an important glycating agent generated in the fructosamine pathway. This is particularly notable because advanced glycation stress is a central driver of diabetic complications, including nephropathy, neuropathy, and vascular damage. Third, through its role in retinoic acid biosynthesis, ALDH1A1 may influence adipose biology, glucose metabolism, and inflammatory tone, all of which are relevant to type 2 diabetes pathophysiology. Taken together, ALDH1A1 stands out as a plausible protective metabolic enzyme that may mitigate oxidative and carbonyl stress in diabetes.[PubMed:12851412](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12851412) [PubMed:17567582](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17567582) [PubMed:26430123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26430123) 

In a related but distinct way, the next protein points toward convergence between neuronal regulation and inflammatory signaling. PTPRS is highly relevant to diabetes because it links neuronal biology, growth factor signaling, and innate immune regulation, all of which are central to diabetic disease progression. Its capacity to attenuate Akt and MAPK signaling suggests a broader role in restraining trophic and survival pathways that overlap conceptually with insulin signaling networks. More importantly, its documented suppression of TLR9-mediated NF-kappa-B activation and inflammatory cytokine production is notable in the context of diabetes, where sterile inflammation contributes to insulin resistance, beta-cell stress, and end-organ damage. In addition, because PTPRS regulates neurite and axonal outgrowth, it may be mechanistically relevant to diabetic neuropathy, a major complication characterized by impaired neuronal maintenance and regeneration. Thus, PTPRS stands out as a candidate modulator at the interface of inflammation, neuronal injury, and growth factor signaling in diabetes.[PubMed:19833921](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19833921) [PubMed:21454754](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21454754) [PubMed:22406547](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22406547) [PubMed:15797710](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15797710) [PubMed:19780196](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19780196) [PubMed:22519304](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22519304) [PubMed:10080191](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10080191) [PubMed:7529177](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7529177) [PubMed:26231120](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26231120) 

Extending this signaling perspective, RET appears relevant because it may connect metabolic control with neuronal trophic support. RET is particularly important in the context of diabetes because it is directly connected to insulin and leptin signaling networks, two central regulators of systemic glucose homeostasis and energy balance. Its ability to facilitate signaling downstream of insulin and IGF1 receptors, and to enhance leptin-triggered JAK2 and IRS1/IRS2 signaling, suggests that it may influence insulin sensitivity, nutrient sensing, and metabolic control. Dysregulation of these pathways is fundamental to obesity-associated insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Furthermore, RET also amplifies neurotrophic signaling pathways, which may be relevant to preservation of peripheral neurons and therefore to diabetic neuropathy. For these reasons, RET stands out as a signaling integrator with plausible influence on both metabolic regulation and diabetes-related neural complications.

A related vascular and neurodevelopmental dimension is suggested by NRP1. NRP1 is relevant to diabetes primarily because abnormal VEGF signaling and microvascular dysfunction are central to diabetic complications, especially diabetic retinopathy, nephropathy, and impaired wound healing. A protein that modulates VEGF-165 availability and vascular integrity is therefore of considerable interest. If NRP1 sequesters VEGF and promotes apoptosis or reduces vessel stability, it could contribute to defective angiogenesis or endothelial dysfunction in some diabetic contexts. Conversely, altered NRP1 activity might also affect pathological neovascular responses, such as those observed in proliferative diabetic retinopathy. Its additional interactions with semaphorin pathways further suggest roles in neurovascular patterning, which is important because diabetes frequently damages both vascular and neural compartments. Thus, NRP1 stands out as a plausible mediator of diabetic microvascular disease.[PubMed:10748121](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10748121) [PubMed:26503042](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26503042) 

Shifting from vascular signaling to immune regulation, ALCAM may be of interest because it combines adaptive immune activation with innate inflammatory sensing. Chronic low-grade inflammation is a defining feature of type 2 diabetes, while immune-mediated tissue injury is central to type 1 diabetes. ALCAM promotes T-cell activation and proliferation and contributes to immunological synapse maturation, making it potentially relevant to autoimmune responses against pancreatic beta cells. In addition, its capacity to bind bacterial products such as LPS and trigger MAPK signaling and pro-inflammatory cytokine release is highly pertinent to metabolic endotoxemia, a process implicated in obesity-associated insulin resistance. Through these dual immune functions, ALCAM may connect microbial inflammatory stimuli and T-cell-mediated immune activation to diabetes pathogenesis.[PubMed:15048703](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15048703) [PubMed:15294938](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15294938) [PubMed:16352806](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16352806) [PubMed:16914752](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16914752) [PubMed:24584089](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24584089) [PubMed:24945728](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24945728) [PubMed:17601777](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17601777) 

From immune regulation, the discussion naturally broadens to endocrine stress adaptation. CRHBP is potentially relevant to diabetes through neuroendocrine stress regulation. The CRF-HPA axis is a major determinant of glucocorticoid secretion, and excess glucocorticoid signaling promotes hepatic glucose production, insulin resistance, visceral adiposity, and gestational metabolic disturbances. By binding and inactivating CRF, CRHBP may buffer excessive pituitary-adrenal activation. This function is especially interesting in pregnancy, where altered endocrine adaptation can contribute to gestational diabetes. Although the connection is less direct than for metabolic enzymes or insulin-pathway adaptors, CRHBP stands out as a plausible endocrine regulator influencing glucose homeostasis under stress and during pregnancy.

A somewhat different but still complication-relevant profile is suggested by MYOC. MYOC is of interest in diabetes because it touches multiple processes implicated in diabetic complications, particularly cytoskeletal remodeling, mitochondrial dysfunction, wound repair, and peripheral nerve biology. Its ability to regulate cell adhesion and migration may be relevant to tissue remodeling and impaired repair responses seen in diabetes. Its involvement in mitochondrial depolarization is also notable, since mitochondrial stress is a major contributor to insulin resistance and diabetic tissue injury. Most importantly, MYOC has a documented role in peripheral nervous system myelination and neurite outgrowth, which makes it potentially relevant to diabetic neuropathy. Although MYOC is not a classical diabetes gene, its functional profile suggests possible importance in complication biology, especially in neural and extracellular matrix-associated pathology.

Continuing with proteins linked to neuronal survival pathways, NTRK3 may be relevant because neurotrophin signaling contributes to neuronal survival, regeneration, and stress responses, all of which are critical in diabetic neuropathy. Its activation of PI3K/AKT and MAPK pathways is particularly important, as these pathways are also central to cell survival and metabolic adaptation. In diabetes, chronic hyperglycemia and oxidative stress impair neuronal trophic support, leading to axonal degeneration and sensory dysfunction. Therefore, proteins such as NTRK3 that sustain survival signaling may influence susceptibility to or progression of diabetic neuropathy. Its role in development is less directly related, but its trophic signaling properties make it a biologically meaningful candidate in diabetes-associated nerve injury.

Closely related to this theme, NTRK2 may also have relevance through regulation of small GTPase signaling, cytoskeletal dynamics, and cell motility. RAC1 and CDC42 are important not only in neuronal morphology but also in insulin-responsive trafficking processes, barrier function, and tissue remodeling. In diabetes, altered cytoskeletal and adhesion signaling contributes to endothelial dysfunction, impaired repair, and neuropathic degeneration. Although the evidence provided here is not specific to glucose metabolism, the functional coupling of extracellular cues to RAC1/CDC42 signaling makes NTRK2 a potentially relevant modulator of diabetes-related cellular stress responses and complication pathways, particularly in neural and vascular tissues.

This emphasis on neural maintenance and repair leads directly to RTN4R. RTN4R is especially relevant to diabetic neuropathy because it regulates axonal maintenance, myelination, neuronal survival, and regenerative inhibition. Diabetic neuropathy involves progressive degeneration of peripheral axons and impaired capacity for repair. A molecule that preserves myelinated axons but also inhibits neurite extension may shape the balance between neuronal stability and regeneration in diabetic nerve injury. Its anti-apoptotic and axon-protective functions suggest potential protective roles, whereas its neurite growth-inhibitory activity may limit recovery once injury occurs. Accordingly, RTN4R stands out as a plausible contributor to the chronic and often irreversible nature of diabetic neuropathy.[PubMed:12089450](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12089450) [PubMed:27922006](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27922006) [PubMed:7533044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7533044) [PubMed:10625334](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10625334) [PubMed:7516497](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7516497) [PubMed:9262180](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9262180) [PubMed:9469574](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9469574) [PubMed:9482781](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482781) [PubMed:9482783](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482783) [PubMed:26335717](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26335717) [PubMed:15953602](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15953602) [PubMed:19158290](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19158290) [PubMed:17640868](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17640868) 

Moving from neural repair toward broader metabolic regulation, MME is potentially relevant to diabetes because the provided function links it to regulation of fat metabolism, a process fundamentally involved in obesity, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes. Endocrine or paracrine factors that influence lipid handling can affect adipose tissue expansion, ectopic lipid deposition, and downstream glucose intolerance. In addition, smooth muscle regulatory effects may be relevant to gastrointestinal motility and vascular function, both of which can be altered in diabetes. Although the present annotation is limited, the connection to metabolic regulation makes MME a protein of interest in the broader context of diabetes pathophysiology.

Finally, GHRL is relevant to diabetes because appetite regulation, gastric emptying, and intestinal motility are tightly linked to postprandial glucose control and energy balance. Hormones that suppress food intake and slow gastric emptying can improve glycemic excursions by reducing nutrient delivery and caloric intake, concepts that are central to modern diabetes therapeutics. The annotation provided here suggests a role in satiety and gastrointestinal regulation, both of which are clinically important in obesity and type 2 diabetes. Therefore, even though the functional description is limited, GHRL stands out as a candidate modulator of metabolic homeostasis.

### Atherosclerosis (HP:0002621) 

Atherosclerosis is a chronic disease of medium-sized and large arteries characterized by lipid accumulation, endothelial injury, inflammatory cell recruitment, smooth muscle cell migration, extracellular matrix remodeling, and formation of fibrofatty plaques within the arterial wall. The process typically begins with endothelial dysfunction, which increases vascular permeability and expression of adhesion molecules, thereby facilitating retention and modification of circulating lipoproteins and recruitment of monocytes and other immune cells into the intima. These cells differentiate into macrophages, take up modified lipids, and form foam cells, which contribute to fatty streaks and later to complex plaques with necrotic cores, fibrous caps, calcification, and variable stability. In diabetes, atherosclerosis is especially important because it underlies much of the excess burden of coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, and peripheral arterial disease. The diabetic milieu promotes every major stage of plaque development through persistent hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, oxidative stress, chronic low-grade inflammation, advanced glycation end product formation, altered protein kinase signaling, endothelial nitric oxide imbalance, innate immune activation, and epigenetic reprogramming of vascular and immune cells. Recent work further indicates that diabetes does not merely coexist with atherosclerosis but may actively accelerate plaque initiation, growth, inflammatory activation, and impaired resolution, making diabetic atherosclerosis a distinct and highly pathogenic vascular state.  

Against this biological background, the collected publications consistently support a close connection between atherosclerosis and diabetes.

The collected publications show that atherosclerosis is tightly linked to diabetes because diabetes creates a metabolic and inflammatory environment that accelerates vascular injury, plaque formation, and plaque destabilization. Multiple reviews consistently identify prolonged hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, oxidative stress, advanced glycation end product signaling, protein kinase activation, and chronic inflammation as central mechanisms by which diabetes promotes endothelial dysfunction and atherogenesis across the arterial wall, with oxidative stress acting as a major upstream driver of inflammatory and redox-sensitive signaling changes. Endothelial dysfunction emerges as an early and unifying event, since high glucose and related metabolic stress increase adhesion molecules, reduce endothelial nitric oxide synthase activity, and favor leukocyte recruitment and vascular inflammation. Several studies specifically implicate the nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain and leucine-rich repeat pyrin domain containing 3 inflammasome and interleukin one beta signaling axis in this process: diabetes patients show increased inflammasome activity and interleukin one beta levels, and these changes correlate with carotid atherosclerosis, while experimental inhibition of this pathway reduces lesion burden, inflammatory gene expression, oxidative stress, and improves vascular function in diabetic atherosclerosis models. Beyond generalized inflammation, diabetes also appears to induce pathway-specific molecular changes in vascular cells. One mechanistic study demonstrated that S-nitrosylation of guanine nucleotide-binding protein G(i) subunit alpha-2 enhances coupling with C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 5, suppresses large tumor suppressor kinase 1 activity, drives yes-associated protein nuclear translocation, and triggers endothelial inflammation, thereby directly promoting diabetes-accelerated atherosclerosis; prevention of this post-translational modification, including by melatonin treatment, attenuated disease progression. Immune cell remodeling is also important: diabetes promotes epigenetic alteration of macrophages through histone deacetylase 3, favoring proinflammatory polarization and worsening plaque development, while persistent neutrophil extracellular traps in diabetes enhance macrophage inflammasome activity and impair plaque resolution even after lipid lowering. Collectively, these studies indicate that atherosclerosis is not simply a complication occurring alongside diabetes, but may represent a biologically integrated consequence of diabetic metabolic stress, innate immune activation, endothelial injury, and maladaptive vascular remodeling, which helps explain the markedly elevated burden of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease in diabetic populations and supports anti-inflammatory, redox-modulating, and cell-targeted therapeutic strategies.[PubMed:34294713](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34294713) [PubMed:35844498](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35844498) [PubMed:35557850](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35557850) [PubMed:30384259](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30384259) [PubMed:28966336](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28966336) [PubMed:32155866](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32155866) [PubMed:40076813](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40076813) [PubMed:37215106](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37215106) [PubMed:30934586](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30934586) [PubMed:34655814](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34655814) [PubMed:31722564](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31722564) [PubMed:31571967](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31571967) [PubMed:34536551](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34536551) [PubMed:32191637](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32191637) [PubMed:33323396](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33323396) [PubMed:32266782](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32266782) [PubMed:34269660](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34269660) [PubMed:34623232](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34623232) 

This literature context also helps frame the enrichment result identified in the present analysis.

There were 15 diabetes-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of atherosclerosis, a chronic arterial disease characterized by lipid accumulation, endothelial injury, inflammatory cell recruitment, smooth muscle cell migration, extracellular matrix remodeling, and fibrofatty plaque formation within medium-sized and large arteries. In the context of diabetes, this enrichment is biologically notable because atherosclerosis accounts for a substantial proportion of excess cardiovascular risk, including coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, and peripheral arterial disease, and because the diabetic metabolic environment promotes essentially every major stage of plaque initiation and progression through persistent hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, oxidative stress, chronic low-grade inflammation, advanced glycation end product formation, altered protein kinase signaling, endothelial nitric oxide imbalance, innate immune activation, and epigenetic reprogramming. The identification of 15 proteins within this pathway therefore supports a concentrated and disease-relevant functional signal linking diabetes to accelerated endothelial dysfunction, immune cell infiltration, foam cell formation, plaque growth, and plaque instability.

To further contextualize this enrichment, the interaction structure of the identified proteins is shown below.

Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 15 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here: [Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=808ABD17EFEA878C).

![PPI Network](imgs/bb7af5ee-e606-4e3e-9fe5-ccf9a7f6015b.png)

Building on this network-level view, the following paragraphs summarize several proteins highlighted during the functional enrichment analysis.

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

GHR is highly relevant to diabetes because the growth hormone axis is a major regulator of systemic insulin sensitivity, hepatic glucose production, and lipid metabolism. A function that increases soluble GHBP and negatively regulates growth hormone signaling is particularly notable, as altered GH signaling can influence insulin resistance, a central pathogenic feature of type 2 diabetes. Excess growth hormone action is known to promote lipolysis and hepatic gluconeogenesis while antagonizing insulin action, whereas attenuation of this pathway may have metabolically protective effects. Therefore, variation in GHR activity or processing could plausibly affect glycemic control and the balance between insulin sensitivity and resistance. Although the provided annotation is concise and does not include a PubMed citation, this protein stands out because endocrine cross-talk between growth hormone and insulin signaling is well established in diabetes pathophysiology.  

From endocrine regulation, the analysis then shifts toward intermediary metabolism and substrate handling.

AGXT is of potential interest in diabetes because it participates in amino acid metabolism linked to pyruvate handling and contributes, albeit weakly, to gluconeogenesis. Hepatic gluconeogenesis is a major determinant of fasting hyperglycemia in diabetes, especially in insulin-resistant states where inappropriate endogenous glucose production persists despite elevated circulating glucose. Even though AGXT is not a canonical diabetes gene, its role in converting substrates connected to pyruvate and serine metabolism suggests a possible contribution to broader metabolic network changes that influence glucose homeostasis. This makes AGXT relevant primarily from a metabolic systems perspective, particularly in relation to hepatic substrate flux and fasting glucose regulation.  

A related but distinct aspect of diabetic pathophysiology involves lipid trafficking and intracellular sterol balance.

NPC2 stands out because disordered intracellular cholesterol trafficking is increasingly recognized as a contributor to metabolic disease, including diabetes. Its central function in mobilizing lysosomal cholesterol and transferring unesterified cholesterol to NPC1 links NPC2 to cellular lipid homeostasis, membrane composition, and organelle stress responses. In diabetes, especially type 2 diabetes, abnormal lipid handling contributes to insulin resistance, hepatosteatosis, inflammation, and beta-cell dysfunction. Lysosomal cholesterol accumulation can disrupt cellular signaling and metabolic flexibility, while the secreted form of NPC2 may additionally influence systemic sterol balance through biliary cholesterol secretion. Thus, although NPC2 is classically associated with lipid storage disorders, its annotated functions have meaningful mechanistic overlap with diabetic dyslipidemia and metabolic stress pathways. The annotation is supported by multiple studies describing cholesterol export and biliary sterol transport.[PubMed:12591949](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12591949) [PubMed:17018531](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17018531) [PubMed:21315718](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21315718) [PubMed:26296895](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26296895) 

Beyond metabolic regulation, several enriched proteins appear to converge on tissue remodeling and fibrotic signaling.

TGFBR2 is one of the most compelling proteins in this list with respect to diabetes because transforming growth factor beta signaling is deeply implicated in diabetic tissue remodeling, fibrosis, inflammation, and vascular complications. Its functions in extracellular matrix production, wound healing, immunosuppression, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition are especially relevant to diabetic nephropathy, retinopathy, cardiomyopathy, and impaired wound repair. Canonical mothers against decapentaplegic homolog dependent signaling downstream of TGFBR2 can drive profibrotic transcriptional programs, while non-canonical signaling can promote apoptosis and cytoskeletal remodeling.
