In chronic hyperglycemia, excessive transforming growth factor beta pathway activation is strongly linked to renal fibrosis and progressive organ damage. Therefore, TGFBR2 stands out as a mechanistically central node connecting diabetes to fibrosis, inflammation, and long-term complications. The provided annotation explicitly cites literature supporting this broad signaling role.[PubMed:33914044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33914044)  

A closely related receptor in the same signaling landscape may further extend these remodeling-related observations.

TGFBR3 is also highly relevant to diabetes because it modulates transforming growth factor beta and bone morphogenetic protein pathway activity, both of which are important in tissue repair, fibrosis, vascular biology, and metabolic regulation. Its roles in cell migration, actin cytoskeletal organization, epithelial adhesion, and epithelial-mesenchymal transformation suggest potential involvement in diabetic wound healing defects, vascular remodeling, and fibrotic complications. In addition, its participation in inhibin signaling and regulation of reproductive physiology may intersect with metabolic-endocrine disturbances that often accompany diabetes. Particularly important is the annotation that TGFBR3 can alter migration and activate partitioning defective 6 homolog, SMAD specific E3 ubiquitin protein ligase 1, and ras homolog family member A signaling during epithelial-mesenchymal transition, processes that may contribute to pathological tissue remodeling under chronic hyperglycemic stress. Thus, TGFBR3 appears important not only as a signaling accessory receptor but also as a regulator of structural cellular responses relevant to diabetic complications.[PubMed:30364975](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30364975) [PubMed:34910520](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34910520)  

Consistent with this emphasis on remodeling, extracellular matrix components also appear among the enriched proteins.

COL3A1 is relevant to diabetes primarily through its structural role in connective tissue and extracellular matrix biology. Although the provided annotation emphasizes developmental neurobiology, type 3 collagen is a major extracellular matrix component and therefore potentially important in diabetic fibrosis, vascular fragility, and wound healing abnormalities. Diabetes is characterized by chronic extracellular matrix remodeling in tissues such as skin, blood vessels, heart, and kidney, and collagens are central mediators of these pathological changes. While COL3A1 is less directly tied to glucose metabolism than GHR or AGXT and less specifically linked to signaling than TGFBR2 or TGFBR3, it remains noteworthy because altered collagen deposition is a hallmark of diabetic complications, particularly impaired tissue repair and fibrotic remodeling.  

Finally, the enrichment profile also points toward coagulation-related biology, which is highly relevant to diabetic vascular disease.

SERPIND1 is potentially relevant to diabetes because thrombotic and vascular abnormalities are major contributors to diabetic morbidity. Its function as a thrombin inhibitor places it within the hemostatic network that influences endothelial function, coagulation balance, and vascular inflammation. Diabetes is associated with a prothrombotic state, increased platelet activation, endothelial dysfunction, and heightened cardiovascular risk. A regulator of thrombin activity may therefore be important in modifying susceptibility to diabetic macrovascular and microvascular complications. Although the annotation does not directly connect SERPIND1 to glucose metabolism, its role in coagulation biology makes it relevant to the vascular disease dimension of diabetes.

### Osteoarthritis (HP:0002758) 

Osteoarthritis is a chronic degenerative disorder of synovial joints characterized by progressive loss of articular cartilage, remodeling of subchondral bone, osteophyte formation, narrowing of the joint space, sclerosis, and, in advanced disease, deformity and substantial functional limitation. Although traditionally viewed as a consequence of mechanical wear, current evidence indicates that osteoarthritis is a whole-joint disease involving cartilage, synovium, subchondral bone, ligaments, menisci, periarticular muscle, and the extracellular matrix. At the tissue level, the disease is driven by an imbalance between anabolic and catabolic processes in chondrocytes, with reduced synthesis of type two collagen and proteoglycans and increased activity of matrix-degrading enzymes and inflammatory mediators. Synovial macrophage-predominant innate immune activation, extracellular matrix damage signals, oxidative stress, altered energy metabolism, and abnormal bone remodeling further promote disease progression. In addition to local biomechanical stress, systemic metabolic factors are increasingly recognized as important modifiers of osteoarthritis risk and severity, especially in people with obesity, insulin resistance, and type two diabetes. These systemic influences include chronic hyperglycemia, advanced glycation end product accumulation, low-grade inflammation, oxidative stress, altered insulin signaling, disordered adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase activity, extracellular matrix glycosylation abnormalities, and complement activation, all of which can impair cartilage homeostasis and worsen joint degeneration.  

Against this biological background, the collected literature supports a biologically plausible and clinically meaningful link between diabetes, especially type two diabetes, and osteoarthritis. Epidemiologic and review studies indicate that diabetes is associated not only with the coexistence of osteoarthritis through shared risk factors such as aging, obesity, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, but also with pathogenic mechanisms that may independently accelerate joint degeneration through chronic hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, oxidative stress, and low-grade inflammation (PubMed:30712918, PubMed:33511986, PubMed:37189487, PubMed:35509632). Mechanistically, insulin normally supports cartilage anabolism by promoting type two collagen and proteoglycan synthesis and restraining matrix breakdown, whereas insulin-resistant states may impair these protective effects and shift joint tissues toward catabolism and extracellular matrix destruction (PubMed:33511986, PubMed:32566279). Diabetes-related accumulation of advanced glycation end products has been repeatedly highlighted as a major contributor to cartilage stiffening, inflammatory activation, and accelerated destruction of cartilage, bone, synovium, tendons, and ligaments, thereby worsening pain and structural progression in osteoarthritis (PubMed:35223234, PubMed:30712918). Molecular profiling further suggests that diabetes modifies osteoarthritis biology at the extracellular matrix level: glycoproteomic analysis of cartilage from patients with osteoarthritis and type two diabetes revealed distinct N-glycosylation abnormalities, enrichment of phosphoinositide three-kinase and protein kinase B signaling, focal adhesion, and extracellular matrix receptor interaction pathways, and increased glycosylated complement component eight alpha chain, which may enhance membrane attack complex activity and aggravate cartilage destruction (PubMed:35484284). Complementary bioinformatic work identified shared differentially expressed genes and pathways between type two diabetes and osteoarthritis, with enrichment in ossification, leukocyte migration, extracellular matrix structure, phosphoinositide three-kinase and protein kinase B signaling, and Wingless-related integration site signaling, and highlighted matrix metallopeptidase nine and angiopoietin-like four as potentially important common mediators (PubMed:39176085). Genetic evidence also supports a shared biological basis, with genome-wide correlation and colocalized association signals implicating lipid metabolism, skeletal formation, and obesity-related loci in the comorbidity between type two diabetes and osteoarthritis (PubMed:37433298). Experimental evidence strengthens this interpretation, as diabetes in mouse models accelerates osteoarthritis progression by deteriorating subchondral bone microarchitecture, mineral composition, biomechanical strength, and bone remodeling balance, thereby worsening the structural environment that supports articular cartilage (PubMed:34268381). Clinically, diabetes in people with osteoarthritis is associated with poorer physical function, particularly for walking, crouching, and prolonged standing, suggesting that the coexistence of both diseases may confer a more disabling phenotype (PubMed:40352459). Therapeutically, antidiabetic treatment may also modify osteoarthritis risk: a large cohort study found that metformin use in adults with type two diabetes was associated with a significantly lower incidence of osteoarthritis compared with sulfonylurea treatment, consistent with the concept that improving metabolic dysfunction and activating adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase may protect joint tissues (PubMed:36939700, PubMed:33668426, PubMed:39200096). Overall, the pathway of osteoarthritis degeneration appears to be related to diabetes through intertwined metabolic, inflammatory, extracellular matrix, and subchondral bone mechanisms that extend beyond simple mechanical loading and may help explain why diabetes can increase osteoarthritis susceptibility, worsen symptoms, and potentially influence response to therapy.[PubMed:36939700](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36939700) [PubMed:35484284](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35484284) [PubMed:33511986](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33511986) [PubMed:32566279](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32566279) [PubMed:39176085](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39176085) [PubMed:40352459](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40352459) [PubMed:37189487](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37189487) [PubMed:33668426](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33668426) [PubMed:39200096](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39200096) [PubMed:35223234](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35223234) [PubMed:30712918](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30712918) [PubMed:37433298](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37433298) [PubMed:35509632](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35509632) [PubMed:34268381](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34268381) 

Consistent with this literature-based framework, there were 14 diabetes-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing osteoarthritis as a chronic degenerative disorder of synovial joints marked by progressive articular cartilage loss, subchondral bone remodeling, osteophyte formation, joint space narrowing, sclerosis, deformity, and substantial functional limitation. This enrichment links diabetes to a whole-joint disease process involving cartilage, synovium, subchondral bone, ligaments, menisci, periarticular muscle, and the extracellular matrix, and is biologically consistent with the recognized contribution of chronic hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, oxidative stress, low-grade inflammation, advanced glycation end product accumulation, altered energy metabolism, abnormal adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase signaling, extracellular matrix glycosylation abnormalities, and complement activation to worsening joint degeneration in metabolic disease.

To further contextualize these enriched proteins, the figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for these 14 proteins, together with the link to the STRING webpage for direct network inspection and further functional exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/4200ad47-18f7-4a5b-9fb9-09d212711589.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=1CDB84388B4047CB)

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified several significant proteins. These proteins may provide a more detailed view of how diabetes-related biology could intersect with osteoarthritis-associated pathways, and they are introduced below in the same order as in the draft.

GHR is among the most directly relevant proteins in this list for diabetes because the growth hormone axis is tightly linked to systemic insulin sensitivity, hepatic glucose production, lipolysis, and overall metabolic homeostasis. Altered growth hormone signaling can promote insulin resistance, a central mechanism in type 2 diabetes, while changes in GHBP production may modulate hormone bioavailability and downstream signaling intensity. Because this protein is described as acting as a negative inhibitor of growth hormone signaling, it is notable in the context of diabetes as a potential regulator of the balance between anabolic growth signals and diabetogenic metabolic effects. Dysregulation of the GH/GHR pathway has long been associated with impaired glucose tolerance and altered insulin action; therefore, among the proteins listed, GHR stands out as having one of the clearest mechanistic connections to diabetes pathophysiology, especially insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction.

In a related but somewhat broader signaling context, BMP4 also appears highly relevant to diabetes because it lies at the intersection of developmental signaling, vascular biology, and intracellular pathways that are central to metabolic disease. The protein initiates canonical SMAD-dependent BMP signaling and can also activate ERK/MAP kinase, PI3K/Akt, and SRC cascades, all of which are pathways with recognized importance in insulin action, cell survival, inflammation, and tissue remodeling. Its documented role in angiogenesis and vascular development is particularly noteworthy, since diabetic complications are strongly driven by microvascular and macrovascular injury. In addition, TGF-beta/BMP family signaling has been implicated in adipose tissue remodeling, pancreatic development, fibrosis, and endothelial dysfunction, making BMP4 a plausible contributor to both the metabolic and complication-related dimensions of diabetes. The broad signaling repertoire of BMP4, together with its capacity to influence vascular responses and transcriptional programs, makes it one of the most biologically compelling proteins in this set for diabetes-related interpretation (PubMed:10049358, PubMed:14973287, PubMed:15206957, PubMed:34995814, PubMed:27713059, PubMed:8898217, PubMed:29148101).[PubMed:10049358](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10049358) [PubMed:14973287](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14973287) [PubMed:15206957](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15206957) [PubMed:34995814](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34995814) [PubMed:27713059](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27713059) [PubMed:8898217](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8898217) [PubMed:29148101](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29148101) 

Shifting from metabolic and vascular signaling to immune regulation, IL2RA is especially important in relation to diabetes because immune tolerance is a central mechanism in autoimmune beta-cell destruction, the defining feature of type 1 diabetes. By controlling TREG activity, IL2RA contributes to the suppression of autoreactive T cells that would otherwise attack self-antigens, including those expressed by pancreatic islets. This makes IL2RA one of the strongest candidates in the list for a meaningful diabetes connection, particularly for type 1 diabetes susceptibility and progression. Defects in IL-2/IL2RA signaling can weaken TREG-mediated immune restraint, thereby favoring chronic autoimmunity and loss of insulin-producing beta cells. Even though no PubMed citations were provided in the source text for this entry, the functional description itself strongly supports its relevance to autoimmune mechanisms in diabetes.

Along similar lines, but with additional links to skeletal and oxidative pathways, TNFRSF11B is notable for diabetes because it links bone remodeling, immune regulation, calcium signaling, and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species generation, all of which can intersect with diabetic disease processes. Its role in dendritic cell and T-cell interactions suggests potential relevance to immune dysregulation, which is particularly important in type 1 diabetes and may also contribute to chronic inflammation in type 2 diabetes. In addition, the induction of intracellular Ca2+ oscillations and mitochondrial ROS generation is mechanistically interesting because calcium homeostasis and oxidative stress are major determinants of beta-cell function, insulin secretion, and tissue injury in diabetes complications. Its established functions in bone resorption are also pertinent, as diabetes is associated with altered bone metabolism and increased skeletal fragility. Thus, TNFRSF11B stands out as a multifunctional mediator that may connect immune, metabolic, and complication-related pathways in diabetes (PubMed:22664871).[PubMed:22664871](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22664871) 

Moving from signaling and immune regulation to extracellular matrix biology, CANT1 has a more indirect but still potentially meaningful connection to diabetes through its role in proteoglycan synthesis. Proteoglycans are major components of the extracellular matrix and vascular basement membranes, structures that are profoundly altered in diabetic complications such as nephropathy, retinopathy, and vasculopathy. Because diabetes is characterized by chronic hyperglycemia-driven matrix remodeling and tissue fibrosis, proteins that influence proteoglycan biosynthesis may contribute to the structural changes underlying long-term organ damage. Although the provided description does not establish a direct role in glucose metabolism or insulin signaling, CANT1 may be relevant in the context of extracellular matrix integrity and diabetic microvascular disease.

Finally, extending this interpretation to hemostatic dysfunction, F9 is relevant to diabetes primarily because diabetes is associated with a prothrombotic state and elevated cardiovascular risk. Hyperglycemia, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and altered platelet and coagulation activity all contribute to vascular events in diabetic patients. As a core component of the intrinsic coagulation cascade, factor IX may therefore be important in understanding the thrombotic complications of diabetes, including accelerated atherosclerotic disease and microvascular injury. While it is not a primary driver of diabetes onset, its function is highly pertinent to the vascular and hemostatic abnormalities that accompany established disease.

### Small intestine; endocrine cells[High] (HPA:0481293) 

The pathway described as small intestine endocrine cells refers to the specialized hormone-secreting epithelial cells dispersed throughout the small intestinal mucosa, including cells that produce glucagon-like peptide one, glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, serotonin, and other metabolically active peptides. Although these cells represent only a minor fraction of the intestinal epithelium, they serve as a major interface between luminal nutrients and systemic metabolic regulation. After sensing carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, bile acids, and microbially derived signals, small intestinal endocrine cells release hormones that regulate pancreatic insulin secretion, appetite, gastric emptying, hepatic glucose production, intestinal transport, and gut-brain communication. This pathway is therefore central to postprandial glucose handling and whole-body energy homeostasis. Recent human and organoid studies further indicate that small intestinal endocrine cells are highly plastic and transcriptionally heterogeneous, with some subsets showing beta cell-like features, including insulin expression during fetal development, and with others being directly targetable by pharmacological, nutritional, microbial, and procedural interventions relevant to diabetes treatment and prevention.  

Against this biological background, the relationship between small intestinal endocrine cells and diabetes appears particularly relevant because these cells influence both insulin-dependent and insulin-independent control of glucose homeostasis, and because their differentiation, hormone output, and plasticity are altered in both type one diabetes and type two diabetes. Reviews of small intestinal nutrient sensing show that nutrient-triggered hormone release from these cells regulates food intake, glucose tolerance, and hepatic glucose production, while obesity and diabetes disrupt these gut-brain and gut-metabolic signaling pathways, establishing the small intestine as an important pathogenic and therapeutic site in metabolic disease (PubMed:33568676). In type two diabetes, human studies demonstrate that jejunal endocrine cells have an impaired differentiation program, with reduced glucagon-like peptide one lineage commitment, reduced proglucagon maturation, and lower glucagon-like peptide one positive cell density, supporting the concept that defective endocrine cell identity contributes to the diminished incretin effect and hyperglycemia in obesity-associated diabetes (PubMed:33037328). Complementing this, duodenal studies in obesity found expansion of glucagon-like peptide one and other endocrine cell populations, yet these increases correlated with poor glycemic indices, suggesting that increased cell number does not necessarily translate into effective hormone action and may reflect compensatory but insufficient adaptation (PubMed:40790227). Several intervention studies further support a causal role of this pathway: bile acid delivery to the ileo-colonic region increased glucagon-like peptide one and improved postprandial glucose and insulin-related measures in human obesity and diabetes, indicating that stimulation of intestinal endocrine signaling can restore metabolic control (PubMed:32344198); similarly, duodenal targeting through bariatric-type interventions or local ablation altered incretin profiles and improved insulin sensitivity, consistent with the recognized metabolic benefits of modifying proximal small intestinal endocrine signaling (PubMed:38320643, PubMed:37778055, PubMed:33208408). In type one diabetes, intestinal involvement is also increasingly evident. Duodenal enteroid studies from pediatric type one diabetes revealed altered epithelial differentiation, increased endocrine cell markers, and impaired barrier and transport properties, indicating that the diabetic intestinal epithelium is remodeled in ways that may influence nutrient sensing, immune signaling, and enteroendocrine function (PubMed:38789719). Moreover, modulation of the intestinal microbiota by fecal microbiota transplantation preserved residual endogenous insulin secretion in recent-onset type one diabetes, and the response was associated with small intestinal microbial and gene expression features, further linking intestinal endocrine-immune-microbial networks to disease progression (PubMed:33106354). Finally, the pathway has regenerative relevance because human fetal small intestine contains enteroendocrine cell subsets that express insulin and other beta cell genes, and experimental work has proposed pharmacological conversion of gut epithelial cells into insulin-producing cells as a treatment strategy for insulin-deficient diabetes, suggesting that small intestinal endocrine cells may serve not only as regulators of glucose metabolism but also as a potential source for beta cell replacement or restoration (PubMed:34887578, PubMed:38426644).[PubMed:33568676](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33568676) [PubMed:33037328](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33037328) [PubMed:40790227](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40790227) [PubMed:32344198](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32344198) [PubMed:38320643](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38320643) [PubMed:37778055](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37778055) [PubMed:33208408](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33208408) [PubMed:38789719](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38789719) [PubMed:33106354](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33106354) [PubMed:34887578](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34887578) [PubMed:38426644](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38426644) 

Consistent with this broader literature, the enrichment analysis identified 51 diabetes-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of small intestine endocrine cells, indicating a substantial concentration of disease-relevant molecular signals within a highly specialized epithelial compartment that, despite representing only a small fraction of the small intestinal mucosa, exerts disproportionately broad control over postprandial glucose regulation, insulin secretion, appetite, gastric emptying, hepatic glucose production, intestinal transport, and gut-brain communication. This enrichment is biologically notable because the pathway integrates nutrient sensing across multiple input classes, including carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, bile acids, and microbially derived signals, and translates these inputs into hormone secretion programs involving glucagon-like peptide one, glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, serotonin, and other metabolically active peptides that are directly relevant to diabetes pathophysiology. The identification of 51 proteins within this pathway further supports the concept that diabetes-related molecular perturbation is not restricted to pancreatic tissue alone, but also extends to intestinal endocrine signaling systems that contribute to whole-body energy homeostasis, with recent human and organoid evidence showing marked cellular plasticity, transcriptional heterogeneity, and even beta cell-like features in selected developmental or inducible states.

To place these pathway-level findings into a network context, the figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for these 51 proteins, together with the direct link to the STRING webpage for interactive exploration of the same network.

![PPI Network](imgs/ff28edcc-1d4c-4574-9f19-e867de67e1c1.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=563866F60DD84E03)

Building on this network overview, the function enrichment analysis highlighted several significant proteins that may help explain how this intestinal endocrine pathway could intersect with diabetes-related biology. We introduce these proteins in detail in the following.

GIP is one of the most directly diabetes-relevant proteins in the list because it is a canonical incretin hormone that enhances glucose-stimulated insulin secretion. This function places it at the center of postprandial glucose homeostasis and beta-cell responsiveness. In type two diabetes, impaired incretin action is a major pathogenic feature, and the insulinotropic effect of GIP is often blunted despite preserved or altered hormone secretion. Therefore, GIP is mechanistically linked to defective meal-induced insulin release, dysglycemia, and therapeutic strategies aimed at incretin pathways. Its inclusion is especially important because it connects intestinal endocrine signaling to pancreatic beta-cell function, a core axis in diabetes pathophysiology.  

In parallel with this hormone-centered mechanism, several additional proteins in the enriched set appear to connect intestinal signaling with systemic glucose and energy regulation through metabolic, transport, and stress-response pathways.

FBP1 stands out because it integrates several processes central to diabetes: hepatic gluconeogenesis, pancreatic beta-cell physiology, and systemic energy balance. As a rate-limiting gluconeogenic enzyme, increased FBP1 activity can contribute to excessive endogenous glucose production, a hallmark of fasting hyperglycemia in type two diabetes. Its additional role in beta-cell glucose sensing and insulin secretion suggests that dysregulation of FBP1 may simultaneously worsen both insulin output and hepatic glucose control. The reported links to appetite and adiposity further broaden its relevance to obesity-associated insulin resistance. Collectively, FBP1 represents a strong mechanistic bridge between altered liver metabolism, beta-cell dysfunction, and whole-body energy imbalance in diabetes.  

PTPRM is highly relevant to diabetes because it directly influences the trafficking of SLC2A4/GLUT4, the principal insulin-responsive glucose transporter in adipose tissue and muscle. By promoting CTNND1 dephosphorylation and facilitating GLUT4 localization to the plasma membrane, PTPRM supports efficient glucose uptake, a process that is defective in insulin resistance and type two diabetes. Its additional role in adipogenic differentiation suggests that it may affect both adipose tissue development and metabolic function. Thus, PTPRM may contribute to diabetes susceptibility through impaired peripheral glucose disposal, making it particularly notable in the context of insulin resistance.[PubMed:10753936](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10753936) [PubMed:17761881](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17761881) [PubMed:21998202](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21998202) 

Extending this metabolic perspective, a number of proteins in the list may be relevant through their effects on lipid handling, postprandial nutrient processing, and membrane composition, all of which are frequently altered in diabetes.

APOA4 is important in diabetes because it participates in triglyceride-rich lipoprotein metabolism, high-density lipoprotein biology, and lipid transport, all of which are frequently disturbed in insulin-resistant states. Diabetic dyslipidemia is characterized by elevated very low-density lipoprotein, altered chylomicron handling, and reduced high-density lipoprotein quality, and APOA4 functions are positioned within these pathways. By affecting lipoprotein lipase activation and lipoprotein remodeling, APOA4 may influence postprandial lipemia, ectopic lipid deposition, and downstream insulin resistance. Its relevance is therefore strongest in the metabolic syndrome and type two diabetes context, where abnormalities in glucose and lipid metabolism are tightly coupled.  

CES1 is notable because it is a major adipose tissue lipase and therefore intersects with lipid mobilization, adipocyte biology, and systemic insulin sensitivity. Altered adipose lipolysis contributes to elevated circulating fatty acids, hepatic steatosis, and insulin resistance, all key features of type two diabetes. CES1-mediated hydrolysis of glycerides and retinyl esters suggests broader roles in nutrient storage and metabolic signaling. In the diabetic setting, dysregulation of CES1 could exacerbate lipotoxic stress and impair the metabolic flexibility of adipose tissue and liver.[PubMed:15220344](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15220344)  

PRAP1 is of interest for diabetes because it promotes intestinal lipid absorption and apolipoprotein B-containing lipoprotein assembly, processes that influence postprandial triglyceride excursions and systemic lipid burden. Excess intestinal lipid delivery and increased apolipoprotein B lipoprotein secretion are strongly linked to insulin resistance, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, and cardiometabolic complications in type two diabetes. Its epithelial protective functions may also be relevant, as intestinal barrier integrity and nutrient handling increasingly are recognized as contributors to metabolic disease. PRAP1 therefore connects gut lipid processing with broader metabolic dysfunction.[PubMed:14583459](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14583459) [PubMed:23235459](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23235459) [PubMed:24374861](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24374861)  

PCYT2 is relevant to diabetes because membrane phospholipid composition is increasingly recognized as a determinant of insulin signaling, organelle function, and metabolic homeostasis. As a key enzyme in phosphatidylethanolamine synthesis, PCYT2 may influence membrane curvature, mitochondrial integrity, and the function of membrane-associated receptors and transporters, including those involved in insulin action. Disturbances in phospholipid metabolism can contribute to lipotoxicity, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and impaired insulin responsiveness. Thus, PCYT2 may be mechanistically linked to diabetes through the regulation of cellular membrane architecture and metabolic resilience.[PubMed:31637422](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31637422) [PubMed:9083101](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9083101)  

From lipid and membrane biology, the analysis then shifts toward proteins that may be relevant through endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis and secretory stress, processes that are often implicated in both insulin resistance and beta-cell dysfunction.

ERN1/IRE1 is one of the most important mechanistic candidates in the list because endoplasmic reticulum stress is a well-established driver of both insulin resistance and pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction. Secretory cells such as beta-cells are especially vulnerable to endoplasmic reticulum proteostatic stress due to the heavy demand for insulin biosynthesis. Persistent ERN1 activation can initially support adaptation through XBP1 splicing and unfolded protein response signaling, but chronic activation may promote inflammatory pathways and cell dysfunction. This makes ERN1 highly relevant to diabetes progression, particularly in the transition from compensatory insulin hypersecretion to beta-cell failure.[PubMed:11175748](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11175748) [PubMed:11779464](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11779464) [PubMed:12637535](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12637535) [PubMed:21317875](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21317875) [PubMed:28128204](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28128204) [PubMed:30118681](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30118681) [PubMed:9637683](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9637683) [PubMed:19328063](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19328063) [PubMed:24508390](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24508390) [PubMed:21884936](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21884936) [PubMed:28067262](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28067262)  

P4HB is potentially important in diabetes because it links protein folding, endoplasmic reticulum proteostasis, and lipoprotein assembly. Proper disulfide bond formation is essential for secretory proteins, including insulin and many membrane proteins involved in metabolism. In addition, its role as a component of MTTP suggests a connection to hepatic and intestinal lipoprotein secretion, which is often dysregulated in insulin-resistant states. Given the central role of endoplasmic reticulum stress in beta-cell failure and the contribution of abnormal lipoprotein metabolism to diabetic complications, P4HB may influence both glycemic control and cardiometabolic risk.[PubMed:21670307](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21670307)  

ENTPD5 is relevant to diabetes because it supports endoplasmic reticulum glycoprotein folding and quality control, processes that are crucial in highly secretory metabolic tissues. Pancreatic beta-cells depend on efficient endoplasmic reticulum function for insulin biosynthesis and processing, and disruption of endoplasmic reticulum quality control contributes to beta-cell stress and apoptosis in diabetes. By facilitating glycoprotein reglucosylation, ENTPD5 may help maintain proteostasis under conditions of high secretory demand. This makes it a plausible modulator of beta-cell fitness and metabolic adaptation.[PubMed:10369669](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10369669) [PubMed:21074248](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21074248)  

In addition to these metabolic and proteostatic mechanisms, several proteins may be notable because they connect the pathway to inflammation, innate immunity, and immunometabolic stress, which are increasingly discussed in diabetes pathogenesis.

IL18 stands out because chronic low-grade inflammation is a major pathogenic component of type two diabetes, while innate immune activation also contributes to beta-cell damage in diabetes more broadly. IL18 activates nuclear factor kappa B-dependent inflammatory programs and amplifies T helper one and natural killer cell responses, linking innate and adaptive immunity. Its release downstream of pyroptosis is particularly relevant because inflammasome activation and gasdermin-mediated inflammatory cell death have been implicated in metabolic tissue inflammation and islet dysfunction. Therefore, IL18 may connect barrier stress, inflammasome biology, and systemic insulin resistance.[PubMed:26638072](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26638072) [PubMed:26638073](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26638073) [PubMed:30392956](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30392956)  

GCHFR is noteworthy because it is linked to non-canonical NLRP3 inflammasome activation, a pathway increasingly implicated in obesity-associated inflammation, insulin resistance, and beta-cell injury. By promoting NLRP3-NEK7 association in response to inflammatory danger signals, GCHFR may amplify innate immune activation in metabolic tissues. This is relevant to diabetes because inflammasome-driven cytokine production and pyroptotic signaling can impair insulin action and contribute to islet inflammation. Although more indirect than classical metabolic enzymes, GCHFR fits an emerging immunometabolic framework of diabetes pathogenesis.  

APEX1 is relevant to diabetes primarily through inflammation and metabolic reprogramming. The described ability to induce glycolysis and inflammatory cytokine expression in monocytes illustrates a broader role in immunometabolic activation, a process that is also central to insulin resistance. Cytokines such as IL1B, TNF, and IL6 are established mediators of impaired insulin signaling and beta-cell stress. While the cited function is presented in the context of viral infection, it highlights a mechanism by which APEX1 could contribute to inflammatory metabolic deterioration, especially in diabetes patients who are more susceptible to severe inflammatory responses.[PubMed:32697943](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32697943)  

Alongside inflammatory signaling, some proteins in the enriched set may also be relevant through their roles in cholesterol transport, adipocyte regulation, intermediary metabolism, and epithelial immune homeostasis.

PDZK1 is of interest in diabetes because it regulates SCARB1 surface expression and thereby influences cholesterol handling and lipoprotein metabolism. Dysregulated cholesterol transport and high-density lipoprotein function are common in insulin resistance and contribute to vascular complications of diabetes. More broadly, scaffold proteins that control membrane localization of transporters can shape epithelial nutrient handling and systemic metabolic homeostasis. PDZK1 may therefore be relevant not only to diabetic dyslipidemia but also to end-organ complications driven by altered lipid metabolism.  

PTGR1 is potentially relevant to diabetes because it modulates prostaglandin metabolism and suppresses PPARG activity, a master regulator of adipogenesis, insulin sensitivity, and lipid storage. PPARG is also the pharmacologic target of thiazolidinediones, underscoring its centrality to glucose homeostasis. By inhibiting adipocyte differentiation and PPARG-dependent transcription, PTGR1 may favor dysfunctional adipose expansion and ectopic lipid deposition, both of which promote insulin resistance. This places PTGR1 at the intersection of inflammatory lipid mediators and adipose tissue metabolic health.  

Although the annotation is brief, GPD1 is still relevant because glycerol-3-phosphate metabolism is central to triglyceride synthesis, redox balance, and hepatic lipid handling. In diabetes and insulin resistance, altered glycerol flux contributes to increased gluconeogenesis and dysregulated lipid storage. As an enzyme in glycerolipid metabolism, GPD1 may influence the partitioning of carbon substrates between glucose production and triglyceride synthesis, thereby affecting both hyperglycemia and steatosis. Its importance is therefore inferred from pathway context rather than from the limited functional note provided here.  

PIGR is indirectly relevant to diabetes because it supports mucosal immunity through polymeric immunoglobulin A and immunoglobulin M transport. Mucosal immune homeostasis and gut barrier integrity are increasingly recognized as contributors to metabolic inflammation, insulin resistance, and obesity-associated dysmetabolism. Changes in intestinal immunity can alter host-microbiome interactions and endotoxin exposure, which in turn influence systemic inflammatory tone. Thus, PIGR may be connected to diabetes through gut-immune-metabolic crosstalk rather than direct glucose regulation.  

Finally, consistent with the broader theme of intestinal barrier maintenance in this pathway, TFF1 is noteworthy in the context of diabetes because preservation of the gastrointestinal mucosal barrier may reduce exposure to luminal inflammatory triggers that promote systemic insulin resistance. Barrier dysfunction and low-grade endotoxemia are increasingly implicated in metabolic disease, especially obesity-associated type two diabetes. By supporting mucous gel stability, TFF1 may contribute to intestinal resilience and limit inflammatory signaling originating from the gut. Its relevance is therefore indirect but conceptually important within current models of metabolic inflammation.

### Pluripotent stem cell differentiation pathway (WP:WP2848) 

The pluripotent stem cell differentiation pathway describes the molecular and cellular program through which pluripotent stem cells, including embryonic stem cells and induced pluripotent stem cells, exit self-renewal and progressively acquire specialized identities. In the context of pancreatic development, this pathway is especially important because it recapitulates the sequential transitions from pluripotency to definitive endoderm, primitive gut tube, pancreatic progenitor, endocrine progenitor, and finally insulin-producing beta-like cells and islet-like structures. This process is controlled by tightly coordinated transcriptional regulators, extracellular matrix signals, and developmental signaling pathways, including wingless-related integration site signaling, bone morphogenetic protein signaling, c-Jun N-terminal kinase signaling, and lineage-defining factors such as forkhead box A2 and neurogenin 3. Studies of human pluripotent stem cell differentiation have shown that endocrine and progenitor compartments emerge as distinct cellular states during in vitro pancreatic specification, and that precise modulation of signaling intensity and timing is required to favor endocrine commitment over alternative fates. In addition, the local pancreatic microenvironment, including mesenchymal and endothelial cues, strongly influences beta-cell differentiation and maturation, while three-dimensional culture systems and biomaterial scaffolds improve structural organization and glucose-responsive insulin secretion. Thus, the pluripotent stem cell differentiation pathway is not only a developmental program but also a translational framework for generating replacement beta cells, modeling diabetes-associated defects in endocrine development and insulin action, and identifying barriers to safe and effective regenerative therapy.

Building on this developmental context, the relevance of this pathway to diabetes becomes more apparent when considering both disease mechanism and therapeutic application. This pathway is closely related to diabetes because diabetes fundamentally involves either loss of functional pancreatic beta cells or defective insulin action, and pluripotent stem cell differentiation provides both a mechanistic model and a therapeutic route to address these abnormalities. In type 1 diabetes, directed differentiation of pluripotent stem cells into islet-like cells has emerged as a replacement strategy for restoring endogenous insulin secretion, with early clinical evidence showing that chemically induced pluripotent stem-cell-derived islets can achieve sustained insulin independence and near-normal glycemic control in a patient with type 1 diabetes, thereby demonstrating the direct therapeutic relevance of this pathway to disease reversal (PubMed:39326417). The disease relevance is further supported by developmental studies showing that successful beta-cell generation depends on accurate control of lineage-specifying signals: non-canonical wingless-related integration site 5A and c-Jun N-terminal kinase signaling, together with suppression of bone morphogenetic protein signaling, promote human beta-cell differentiation and maturation, while inhibition of wingless-related integration site signaling increases endocrine differentiation, indicating that dysregulation of these developmental branches can alter beta-cell yield and identity (PubMed:35414140, PubMed:31116975). Genetic evidence also links this pathway to diabetes susceptibility, since forkhead box A2 deficiency in human induced pluripotent stem cells causes defective pancreatic endocrine development, reduced expression of key beta-cell genes, and aberrant activation of wingless-related integration site-associated programs, supporting the concept that impaired differentiation itself can be a cause of diabetes (PubMed:33473118). Beyond type 1 diabetes, pluripotent stem cell differentiation is informative for type 2 diabetes because induced pluripotent stem-cell-derived hepatocytes from affected individuals retain cell-intrinsic insulin signaling defects, including reduced phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase and protein kinase B signaling and increased rho-associated coiled-coil containing protein kinase activity, showing that patient-derived differentiated cells can capture pathogenic insulin resistance mechanisms (PubMed:40231468). Additional work indicates that patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cells can reveal reduced developmental potency toward pancreatic progenitors and greater susceptibility to tacrolimus toxicity in individuals who later develop diabetes after kidney transplantation, suggesting that this pathway also reflects inherited or acquired predisposition to beta-cell failure (PubMed:37448282). At the translational level, optimization of differentiation conditions with extracellular matrix engineering, such as esterified collagen hydrogel, improves endocrine gene expression, cluster integrity, and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, emphasizing that maturation of stem-cell-derived beta cells is a critical determinant of therapeutic efficacy (PubMed:39443977). However, the pathway is also linked to major safety concerns, because incomplete differentiation and persistence of undifferentiated pluripotent cells can lead to teratoma formation after induced pluripotent stem cell-derived beta-cell therapy, highlighting the necessity for rigorous control of lineage commitment before clinical use (PubMed:35018826). Collectively, these studies show that the pluripotent stem cell differentiation pathway is related to diabetes at multiple levels: it governs beta-cell formation, reveals developmental and insulin-resistance defects underlying disease, enables personalized disease modeling, and provides a realistic but still technically challenging platform for regenerative treatment.[PubMed:39326417](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39326417) [PubMed:40231468](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40231468) [PubMed:35414140](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35414140) [PubMed:31116975](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31116975) [PubMed:33473118](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33473118) [PubMed:37448282](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37448282) [PubMed:39443977](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39443977) [PubMed:35018826](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35018826) 

With this broader disease relevance in mind, the enrichment results provide a more focused view of how strongly this pathway may intersect with diabetes-associated biology. There were 15 diabetes-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pluripotent stem cell differentiation pathway, a developmental program that quantitatively spans the stepwise transition from pluripotent stem cells to definitive endoderm, primitive gut tube, pancreatic progenitor, endocrine progenitor, and ultimately insulin-producing beta-like cells and islet-like structures. In diabetes, this enrichment is biologically important because the pathway integrates multiple regulatory layers, including wingless-related integration site signaling, bone morphogenetic protein signaling, c-Jun N-terminal kinase signaling, extracellular matrix control, and lineage-specifying transcription factors such as forkhead box A2 and neurogenin 3, all of which collectively determine whether differentiating cells proceed toward endocrine commitment or diverge into alternative fates. The identification of 15 proteins within this pathway supports a concentrated functional signal linking diabetes to impaired beta-cell generation, endocrine maturation, insulin secretion competence, and regenerative capacity, particularly because this pathway provides the experimental framework used to model diabetes-related defects in pancreatic development and to optimize cell replacement strategies through three-dimensional culture systems, biomaterial scaffolds, and microenvironmental mesenchymal and endothelial cues.

To complement this enrichment result, the interaction network below provides a visual summary of the relationships among these proteins and offers an additional layer for interpretation.

The figure below shows the protein-protein interaction network of these 15 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for interactive inspection.

![PPI Network](imgs/8b5435b8-8b33-4820-ac9e-606737de1c91.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=1B9B3ED3DE5CA8A6)

Following this network-level overview, the enriched proteins can be considered individually to clarify how each may contribute to diabetes-related mechanisms. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the listed proteins, BMP4 stands out because its signaling profile intersects with several biological processes that are highly relevant to diabetes, particularly vascular dysfunction, tissue remodeling, and metabolic stress responses. Diabetes is characterized not only by impaired glucose homeostasis but also by progressive microvascular and macrovascular injury, defective wound healing, and altered tissue repair. BMP4 is notable in this context because it regulates vascular development and angiogenesis and can activate both canonical SMAD-dependent pathways and non-canonical signaling routes, including phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase and protein kinase B and SRC, which are central to endothelial survival and vascular adaptation. Particularly relevant is the observation that BMP4 can induce SRC phosphorylation and activate vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2, linking it mechanistically to pro-angiogenic signaling. This is important for diabetic complications such as retinopathy, nephropathy, and impaired wound healing, where abnormal angiogenesis and endothelial dysfunction are major pathogenic features. In addition, BMP4 belongs to a broader signaling family that has been implicated in inflammation, fibrosis, and vascular calcification, all of which are common in diabetes. Thus, even though the provided annotation emphasizes developmental biology, the vascular and signaling functions of BMP4 may make it a plausible contributor to diabetes-associated endothelial injury and maladaptive angiogenic remodeling.[PubMed:10049358](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10049358) [PubMed:14973287](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14973287) [PubMed:15206957](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15206957) [PubMed:34995814](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34995814) [PubMed:27713059](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27713059) [PubMed:8898217](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8898217) [PubMed:29148101](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29148101) 

In a related way, NOTCH1 may also connect developmental regulation with vascular pathology in diabetes. NOTCH1 is highly relevant to diabetes because it integrates cell-fate control with vascular homeostasis, two processes that are deeply disturbed in diabetic disease. The most compelling diabetes-related aspect of NOTCH1 in the provided annotation is its role in angiogenesis, specifically its ability to negatively regulate endothelial proliferation, migration, and sprouting. This is directly pertinent to diabetic microvascular complications, where endothelial dysfunction, aberrant angiogenesis, and impaired vascular repair are central mechanisms. For example, diabetic retinopathy involves pathological neovascular responses, whereas diabetic wound healing is marked by insufficient or dysregulated vessel formation; altered NOTCH1 signaling could plausibly contribute to both settings by changing the balance between quiescent and activated endothelial states. Beyond vasculature, NOTCH1 governs differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis, processes that are also relevant to pancreatic tissue remodeling, immune regulation, and fibrosis in diabetes. Its broader developmental and cell-specification roles further support the view that dysregulated NOTCH signaling may influence tissue adaptation under chronic hyperglycemic stress. Therefore, NOTCH1 stands out as a strong candidate linking diabetes to abnormal endothelial behavior and defective tissue repair.

Extending this perspective from signaling control to extracellular metabolic regulation, NT5E may be relevant through its effects on the local inflammatory and vascular environment. NT5E is potentially relevant to diabetes because it is a key regulator of extracellular nucleotide metabolism, particularly through the conversion of adenosine monophosphate to adenosine. Although the provided annotation is primarily enzymatic, this function has important pathophysiological implications. Extracellular adenosine is a major signaling molecule that modulates inflammation, vascular tone, endothelial barrier function, and tissue protection during metabolic stress. These processes are highly relevant to diabetes, where chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, ischemia, and altered tissue perfusion contribute to complications in the kidney, retina, heart, and peripheral tissues. By shaping the extracellular balance between pro-inflammatory nucleotides and anti-inflammatory or vasoregulatory nucleosides, NT5E may influence the local tissue environment in diabetes. Its ability to hydrolyze nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide and nicotinamide mononucleotide is also noteworthy because these metabolites are linked to cellular energy homeostasis and redox biology, both of which are disrupted in diabetes. Therefore, while NT5E is not a classic diabetes gene in this list, its metabolic and purinergic regulatory functions may make it mechanistically relevant to diabetic vascular injury and chronic inflammatory stress.[PubMed:8224905](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8224905) 

From extracellular metabolism, the analysis then shifts to coagulation biology, which is also central to diabetic complications. TF is particularly important in diabetes because hypercoagulability and thrombo-inflammatory activation are hallmarks of the diabetic state. The core function of TF as the initiator of the extrinsic coagulation cascade makes it directly relevant to the increased risk of atherothrombosis, myocardial infarction, stroke, and microvascular occlusion observed in patients with diabetes. In diabetic tissues, endothelial injury, inflammation, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysfunction can promote a prothrombotic environment, and TF is a central molecular trigger of this response. Its capacity to activate factors nine and ten through the TF:factor seven a complex places it at the apex of coagulation initiation, meaning that dysregulation of TF expression or activity can have amplified downstream effects on thrombin generation and fibrin formation. This is especially meaningful in diabetes, where coagulation abnormalities intersect with vascular inflammation and endothelial dysfunction to accelerate cardiovascular complications. Accordingly, TF stands out as one of the most clinically relevant proteins in the list because it connects diabetes to one of its most serious outcomes: heightened thrombotic risk.

Finally, VEGFA provides perhaps the clearest bridge between the enriched pathway and the vascular complications that dominate diabetes morbidity. VEGFA is arguably the most directly diabetes-relevant protein in the list because its annotated functions map closely onto the vascular abnormalities that define many diabetic complications. Its central roles in angiogenesis, vascular permeability, endothelial survival, migration, and nitric oxide signaling are especially important in diabetic retinopathy, diabetic nephropathy, and impaired wound healing. In diabetic retinopathy, excessive vascular endothelial growth factor pathway activation is strongly associated with pathological neovascularization and increased vascular permeability, leading to retinal edema and vision loss. The annotation also emphasizes activation of protein kinase B, mitogen-activated protein kinase and extracellular signal-regulated kinase, SRC, focal adhesion kinase, and nitric oxide synthase pathways, all of which are critical mediators of endothelial responses to injury and metabolic stress. These signaling outputs are highly relevant to diabetes, where chronic hyperglycemia disrupts endothelial homeostasis, impairs nitric oxide bioavailability, and promotes abnormal vessel remodeling. The mention of isoforms that can act as decoy receptors is also notable, as it suggests a built-in regulatory mechanism that may influence the balance between physiological and pathological angiogenesis. Overall, VEGFA stands out as a major mechanistic and clinical link to diabetes because it directly governs the vascular leakage, aberrant angiogenesis, and endothelial dysfunction that underlie several of the most consequential diabetic complications.

### carbohydrate binding (GO:0030246) 

Carbohydrate binding refers to the selective physical interaction of proteins or other biomolecules with carbohydrate structures, including simple sugars, complex oligosaccharides, polysaccharides, and chemically modified sugar derivatives. In biology, this function is classically mediated by lectins and other sugar-recognition domains that detect specific glycan patterns on soluble molecules, cell surfaces, extracellular matrix components, pathogens, or damaged self-tissues. Carbohydrate binding therefore represents a fundamental mechanism for molecular recognition, nutrient sensing, cell-cell communication, immune surveillance, and metabolic regulation. In metabolic tissues, carbohydrate-responsive systems also include intracellular glucose-sensing regulators that translate carbohydrate availability into transcriptional programs controlling glycolysis, lipogenesis, storage, and hormone secretion. In the context of diabetes, carbohydrate binding appears to have several biologically important dimensions. First, binding of dietary carbohydrates or carbohydrate-containing substrates may influence digestion and postprandial glucose excursions. Second, recognition of altered glycated or hyperglycemia-modified self-structures may activate inflammatory and complement pathways. Third, intracellular sensing of carbohydrate-derived metabolites regulates gene expression programs that shape insulin secretion, hepatic lipid synthesis, and insulin sensitivity. Fourth, pathological sugar-derived modifications such as advanced glycation can generate neoepitopes that alter immune recognition. Taken together, carbohydrate binding is better understood not as a single linear pathway, but as a broader functional theme linking nutrient handling, glucose sensing, innate immunity, tissue injury, and diabetic complications.  

Building on this conceptual framework, the collected literature suggests that carbohydrate binding is related to diabetes through both metabolic regulation and tissue-damaging inflammatory mechanisms. On the metabolic side, carbohydrate-binding lectins have been proposed as antihyperglycemic agents because they can interact with carbohydrates and diabetes-relevant proteins, with reported effects on blood glucose, oxidative stress, beta cell proliferation, insulin resistance, and inhibition of carbohydrate-digesting enzymes. These observations suggest that sugar recognition may directly influence glycemic control and postprandial carbohydrate handling (PubMed:39323638). This interpretation is consistent with broader therapeutic strategies targeting carbohydrate-processing enzymes such as alpha-glucosidase and alpha-amylase to reduce glucose absorption after meals, as highlighted by studies on repurposed alpha-glucosidase inhibitors and natural inhibitory peptides, as well as by evidence that anthocyanins suppress these digestive enzymes while improving insulin sensitivity and glucose utilization (PubMed:37111312, PubMed:29521054). At the cellular level, carbohydrate sensing is strongly linked to the carbohydrate-responsive element-binding protein, a glucose-responsive transcription factor that detects intracellular carbohydrate availability and regulates gene programs involved in de novo lipogenesis, hepatic metabolic remodeling, and pancreatic islet responses. Dysregulation of this carbohydrate-sensing system has been implicated in type two diabetes mellitus, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, and altered beta cell gene expression in diabetes (PubMed:37055547, PubMed:27900263). In parallel, the inflammatory dimension of carbohydrate binding may also be important. Carbohydrate-binding molecules of innate immunity, particularly mannan-binding lectin and its associated serine proteases, are increased or show enhanced autoreactivity in diabetes, where they appear to recognize hyperglycemia-induced altered self-structures in the kidney and may promote complement activation, thrombogenicity, and diabetic nephropathy. Importantly, their levels correlate with glycemic control, linking abnormal carbohydrate recognition to vascular and renal complications (PubMed:26977416, PubMed:28349070, PubMed:25533914). This broader pathogenic theme is further supported by evidence that hyperglycemia-driven glycation generates structurally altered hemoglobin carrying neoepitopes recognized by circulating autoantibodies in diabetes, indicating that excessive sugar modification creates new carbohydrate-related recognition targets for the immune system (PubMed:30834437). Finally, high glucose also enhances O-linked N-acetylglucosamine modification of signaling proteins such as the mineralocorticoid receptor, stabilizing receptor activity and contributing to diabetic complications. This observation suggests that sugar-derived molecular recognition and modification may extend beyond extracellular lectin biology into intracellular stress signaling (PubMed:38789539). Taken together, the carbohydrate-binding theme appears to be related to diabetes because it connects dietary carbohydrate processing, intracellular glucose sensing, immune recognition of hyperglycemia-altered structures, and the development of chronic complications.[PubMed:39323638](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39323638) [PubMed:37055547](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37055547) [PubMed:37111312](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37111312) [PubMed:29521054](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29521054) [PubMed:26977416](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26977416) [PubMed:28349070](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28349070) [PubMed:27900263](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27900263) [PubMed:25533914](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25533914) [PubMed:30834437](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30834437) [PubMed:38789539](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38789539) 

Consistent with this literature-based interpretation, there were 33 diabetes-associated proteins significantly enriched in the functional theme of carbohydrate binding. This biologically broad process encompasses selective molecular interactions with sugars, oligosaccharides, polysaccharides, and chemically modified carbohydrate derivatives, and it is highly relevant to diabetes because it connects nutrient sensing, postprandial glucose handling, inflammatory recognition of glycated structures, metabolic gene regulation, and tissue injury associated with chronic hyperglycemia. Given that this enriched set contains 33 proteins, the signal supports a substantial convergence of diabetes-related biology on carbohydrate-recognition mechanisms rather than an isolated single-protein effect. This pattern suggests that multiple components of glucose-responsive, glycan-recognition, and damage-sensing systems may collectively contribute to disease pathophysiology.

To further contextualize this enrichment result, the figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for these 33 proteins, together with the direct link to the STRING webpage for interactive network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/22c13c8a-01f5-4b41-a509-934ec3da94d9.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=1359FFC900183889)

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified several significant proteins. These proteins are introduced in more detail below, with each description framed in relation to the broader carbohydrate-binding theme and its possible relevance to diabetes.  

KHK is among the proteins most directly relevant to diabetes because it controls the first committed step of fructose metabolism. Excess fructose exposure has been strongly implicated in metabolic dysfunction, including hepatic lipid accumulation, insulin resistance, and worsening glycemic control. By converting fructose to fructose-1-phosphate, KHK promotes rapid fructose utilization in liver and other tissues, a process that can enhance de novo lipogenesis, adenosine triphosphate depletion, and downstream metabolic stress. In the context of diabetes, this makes KHK mechanistically important as a potential link between dietary sugar excess and metabolic syndrome, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, and type two diabetes pathophysiology.  

Closely related to this carbohydrate-overload axis, SORD is highly relevant to diabetes because the polyol pathway is a classic mediator of hyperglycemia-induced tissue injury. Under diabetic conditions, excess glucose is shunted into sorbitol metabolism, and SORD converts sorbitol to fructose. This pathway contributes to osmotic stress, redox imbalance, and accumulation of reactive metabolites in tissues vulnerable to diabetic complications, including peripheral nerve, retina, and kidney. The production of fructose by SORD may further amplify local metabolic stress and glycation-related damage. Therefore, SORD appears particularly important as a mechanistic link between chronic hyperglycemia and diabetic microvascular complications.[PubMed:6852349](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6852349) [PubMed:18799757](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18799757) 

Moving from intracellular sugar metabolism to glycoprotein handling at the organ level, ASGR1 is of interest in diabetes because it participates in hepatic clearance of desialylated glycoproteins, thereby connecting glycan remodeling to systemic metabolism. Diabetes is associated with altered protein glycosylation and increased glycation, both of which can influence circulating protein turnover and liver handling of modified plasma proteins. As a hepatocyte receptor for terminal galactose- and N-acetylgalactosamine-bearing ligands, ASGR1 may affect the clearance of metabolically relevant glycoproteins and inflammatory mediators. This is especially meaningful because the liver is central to insulin sensitivity, glucose homeostasis, and dyslipidemia in type two diabetes.  

In a related manner, FUOM stands out because it supports guanosine diphosphate-fucose production for protein and lipid fucosylation, a major glycosylation process with broad effects on receptor biology, immune regulation, and intercellular signaling. Aberrant glycosylation is increasingly recognized in diabetes, where altered fucosylation can influence insulin receptor signaling, inflammatory pathways, and endothelial function. Given that diabetes is characterized not only by abnormal glucose metabolism but also by substantial remodeling of the glycoproteome, FUOM may be relevant to both metabolic dysregulation and diabetic vascular complications through its role in generating substrates for nitrogen-linked and oxygen-linked glycan fucosylation.  

Extending from glycan processing to extracellular signaling, PTN is potentially important in diabetes because it integrates extracellular matrix signaling, growth control, vascular responses, and tissue regeneration. The protein binds chondroitin sulfate-containing proteoglycans and receptors such as PTPRZ1 and ALK, activating pathways including phosphoinositide three-kinase and protein kinase B, as well as mitogen-activated protein kinase (PubMed:27445335, PubMed:30497772). These signaling axes are central to insulin action, cell survival, and tissue remodeling. Moreover, PTN has documented roles in hematopoietic regeneration and hemostatic regulation (PubMed:21791434), both of which are relevant to diabetes, a disease associated with chronic inflammation, impaired repair, and vascular dysfunction. Its functions in neuron biology also make it noteworthy in relation to diabetic neuropathy and altered neural plasticity.[PubMed:15121180](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15121180) [PubMed:19442624](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19442624) [PubMed:27445335](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27445335) [PubMed:30497772](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30497772) [PubMed:11414790](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11414790) [PubMed:25000129](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25000129) [PubMed:21791434](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21791434) [PubMed:16619002](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16619002) [PubMed:17121547](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17121547) [PubMed:28657144](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28657144) 

Along similar lines of glycan-dependent signaling, LGALS9 is relevant to diabetes primarily through immunometabolic and vascular mechanisms. Galectins are glycan-binding proteins that regulate inflammation, cell death, and immune tolerance, all of which are increasingly recognized as central to diabetes progression. The ability of LGALS9 to suppress interferon gamma production by natural killer cells suggests a role in modulating inflammatory tone, whereas its anti-angiogenic activity may be particularly relevant to diabetic vascular disease and tissue repair. Since diabetes involves chronic low-grade inflammation together with aberrant angiogenesis in tissues such as retina, kidney, and ischemic wounds, LGALS9 may participate in pathways that shape both immune dysfunction and end-organ complications.  

This immunovascular perspective is further supported by COLEC12, which is notable in diabetes because it directly links innate immunity, endothelial biology, and oxidized lipid handling. The capacity to recognize and internalize oxidized low-density lipoprotein is particularly important, as oxidative stress and modified lipoproteins are major drivers of endothelial dysfunction and accelerated atherosclerosis in diabetes. In addition, diabetic patients exhibit increased susceptibility to infection, making scavenger receptors involved in microbial recognition and phagocytosis biologically relevant. Thus, COLEC12 may contribute to both macrovascular complications and impaired host defense, two clinically important dimensions of diabetes.  

From the standpoint of immune regulation, FCER2 is relevant to diabetes because adaptive and innate immune dysregulation contribute to both type one and type two diabetes. Its roles in B-cell differentiation and antigen presentation suggest potential importance in shaping immune responses, including autoimmunity and chronic inflammation. Furthermore, macrophage activation through nitric oxide-related pathways may intersect with inflammatory tissue injury and metabolic dysfunction. Although FCER2 is not a canonical diabetes gene, its immunoregulatory properties make it a plausible contributor to the inflammatory environment that promotes beta-cell stress, insulin resistance, or altered infection responses in diabetic individuals.  

A somewhat different but still relevant layer of regulation is suggested for MRC1. Although the provided annotation for MRC1 describes a chromatin remodeling function rather than the canonical mannose receptor biology, it still has potential relevance to diabetes through epigenetic regulation. Diabetes is increasingly understood as a disease influenced by persistent transcriptional reprogramming in metabolic, immune, and vascular cells. Chromatin remodeling complexes can shape lineage commitment, inflammatory responses, and stress adaptation, thereby influencing susceptibility to insulin resistance and diabetic complications. The strong neural developmental role also raises possible relevance to diabetic neuropathy and nervous system adaptation to chronic metabolic stress.  

At the tissue-remodeling level, GUSB may be relevant to diabetes because extracellular matrix remodeling and glycosaminoglycan turnover are important in diabetic nephropathy, vascular stiffening, and tissue fibrosis. By participating in degradation of dermatan sulfate and keratan sulfate, GUSB influences the composition of proteoglycan-rich matrices that regulate growth factor availability, filtration barrier integrity, and inflammatory signaling. Altered glycosaminoglycan metabolism has been implicated in diabetic kidney disease and impaired wound healing, making GUSB a potentially informative marker of matrix dysregulation in chronic hyperglycemia.  

In addition to soft-tissue and vascular remodeling, skeletal complications may also be relevant within this enriched set. SOST is of particular interest in diabetes because skeletal fragility is increasingly recognized as a complication of both type one and type two diabetes. By inhibiting Wnt signaling, SOST suppresses osteoblast activity and bone formation, a mechanism highly relevant to diabetic bone disease, where bone quality may be impaired even when bone mineral density is preserved. Wnt signaling also intersects with broader metabolic regulation, suggesting that SOST may sit at the interface of bone-endocrine and glucose-metabolic pathways. Its role therefore may extend beyond bone remodeling to the systemic complications of diabetes.  

Finally, AMBP is relevant to diabetes because coagulation abnormalities and heightened thrombotic risk are major features of the disease, especially in type two diabetes and diabetic vascular complications. A protein capable of inhibiting factor ten a and prothrombin activation may influence the hypercoagulable state associated with endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and atherosclerosis. Its additional inhibition of mast cell proteases also suggests a possible role in inflammatory regulation. Accordingly, AMBP may be important for understanding how protease control intersects with diabetic vasculopathy and thrombosis.

### Complement system (WP:WP2806) 

The complement system is a central arm of innate immunity composed of soluble plasma proteins, membrane-associated receptors, and regulatory factors that together detect danger, amplify inflammatory signaling, opsonize targets for phagocytosis, recruit leukocytes, and directly injure susceptible cells through membrane attack complex formation. Complement activation proceeds through the classical pathway, the lectin pathway, and the alternative pathway, all of which converge on cleavage of complement component three, followed by generation of downstream effector fragments such as complement component three a, complement component five a, and terminal complement complexes. Beyond host defense against infection, the complement system has major homeostatic functions in immune complex clearance, apoptotic cell disposal, shaping of adaptive immunity, tissue remodeling, and metabolic regulation. Tight regulation is essential because excessive or misplaced activation can produce chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, thrombogenicity, and parenchymal injury. Recent work further indicates that complement is not only liver-derived and circulating, but can also be produced and activated locally within tissues and even intracellularly, where it influences cellular metabolism, transcriptional programs, autophagy, inflammatory tone, fibrosis, and repair. This broader biological scope makes the complement system highly relevant to chronic metabolic disease, including autoimmune beta cell destruction, insulin resistance, diabetic kidney disease, diabetic retinal disease, and neurocognitive complications associated with diabetes.

Against this biological background, the collected literature suggests that the complement system is related to diabetes at multiple stages of disease initiation, progression, and complication development. In type one diabetes, complement appears to participate in autoimmune susceptibility and early disease evolution. Genetic studies implicate variation linked to complement component four a and complement component four b in differential risk within the human leukocyte antigen region, suggesting that complement-related immune regulation may modify disease predisposition and endotype structure, particularly in individuals whose first autoantibody targets insulin (PubMed:41627183). Additional studies indicate that disruption of complement biology may precede clinical disease, because children who later develop islet autoimmunity and progress to type one diabetes exhibit reduced levels of multiple complement proteins before autoantibody detection and through disease onset, supporting complement proteins as early biomarkers and possible mechanistic participants in beta cell autoimmunity (PubMed:38303689). This interpretation is further supported by glycomic and genetic evidence linking complement component three variation and altered glycosylation to recent-onset type one diabetes, implying that complement structure and activation state may influence inflammatory potential and disease susceptibility (PubMed:36907892, PubMed:36031042). 

A related but broader pattern is described in type two diabetes, where the association appears to extend more strongly into metabolic dysfunction. Reviews and clinical studies describe complement activation as a feature of obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and hyperglycemia, with circulating complement component one q, complement component three, complement component four, complement factor h, and complement component three b associated with glycemic control, lipid abnormalities, beta cell function, and insulin resistance, and with evidence suggesting that the alternative pathway may be particularly relevant in type two diabetes (PubMed:31938469, PubMed:35370615, PubMed:40967136). Complement-related adipokines may also contribute to metabolic risk, as Mendelian randomization suggested a possible causal role of adipsin in type two diabetes and causal effects of inflammatory mediators on insulin sensitivity and beta cell function in African populations (PubMed:38049854). 

This metabolic and inflammatory framework becomes especially important when considering diabetic complications, where the translational evidence appears strongest.
