Diabetic kidney disease is particularly well supported, as urinary complement proteins including complement component two, complement component five a, collectin kidney one, complement component six, complement factor h, and complement component seven robustly predict progression to kidney failure in both type one and type two diabetes, while kidney tissue studies demonstrate increased complement protein abundance and local expression within diseased diabetic kidneys (PubMed:40775226). Consistently, glomerular deposition of complement component four c in biopsy-proven diabetic kidney disease is associated with heavier proteinuria, more inflammation, and faster progression to end-stage kidney disease, identifying complement activation as a marker and likely mediator of renal injury (PubMed:32983156). Broader kidney literature further supports a pathogenic role for local complement activation in fibrosis and chronic kidney disease progression, which is highly relevant to diabetic nephropathy (PubMed:40519169, PubMed:37735215). Complement dysregulation has also been linked to diabetic retinal disease and to cognitive impairment in diabetes, including elevated complement proteins in astrocyte-derived exosomes from people with type one diabetes and mild cognitive impairment, suggesting that complement-mediated neuroinflammation may contribute to extra-renal diabetic complications (PubMed:38690727, PubMed:37271220). Taken together, the available evidence supports the view that the complement system may represent more than a bystander in diabetes, instead plausibly acting as a mechanistic bridge between innate immunity, autoimmunity, metabolism, inflammation, and tissue injury across both major forms of diabetes and their chronic complications.[PubMed:41627183](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41627183) [PubMed:37649398](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37649398) [PubMed:40775226](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40775226) [PubMed:35370615](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35370615) [PubMed:38049854](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38049854) [PubMed:38690727](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38690727) [PubMed:32983156](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32983156) [PubMed:40519170](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40519170) [PubMed:31400630](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31400630) [PubMed:40519169](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40519169) [PubMed:31938469](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31938469) [PubMed:36907892](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36907892) [PubMed:38303689](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38303689) [PubMed:40967136](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40967136) [PubMed:37735215](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37735215) [PubMed:36031042](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36031042) [PubMed:37271220](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37271220) 

Consistent with this literature context, there were 25 diabetes-associated proteins significantly enriched in the complement system pathway, a core innate immune program that integrates soluble plasma proteins, membrane-associated receptors, and regulatory factors to detect danger signals, amplify inflammation, promote opsonization, recruit leukocytes, and induce target cell injury through terminal complement complex formation. Enrichment across 25 proteins suggests a substantial concentration of diabetes-related molecular signals within a single immunometabolic pathway, which is in line with the broad contribution of complement activation to autoimmune beta cell injury, insulin resistance, diabetic kidney disease, diabetic retinal disease, and neurocognitive complications associated with diabetes. The pathway biology is quantitatively notable because it spans 3 major activation routes, namely the classical pathway, the lectin pathway, and the alternative pathway, which converge on complement component three cleavage and subsequently generate multiple downstream effector fragments, including complement component three a, complement component five a, and terminal complement complexes. In the context of diabetes, the enrichment of 25 proteins in this pathway supports the interpretation that dysregulated complement activity may contribute not only to host defense imbalance, but also to chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, thrombogenicity, tissue remodeling, fibrosis, and altered metabolic regulation.

To further contextualize this enrichment, the figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for these 25 enriched proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for interactive exploration of the network topology and functional connectivity.

![PPI Network](imgs/525bba34-9a62-4a8f-a377-aac41c6bf106.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=8834E81B7E090887)

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We introduce them in detail below.

ADIPOQ is the most directly relevant protein in this set with respect to diabetes because it encodes adiponectin, a canonical adipokine that links adipose tissue biology to systemic glucose and lipid homeostasis. The reported activation of adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase and protein kinase B is particularly important, as these pathways are central regulators of insulin sensitivity, glucose uptake, fatty acid oxidation, and metabolic stress responses. In the context of type two diabetes, reduced adiponectin signaling is strongly associated with insulin resistance, ectopic lipid accumulation, and chronic low-grade inflammation. Therefore, a protein whose core function is to stimulate adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase and protein kinase B signaling stands out as mechanistically connected to improved metabolic control and protection from diabetic pathology. Its additional engagement of mitogen-activated protein kinase suggests broader effects on cell survival and metabolic adaptation. Overall, ADIPOQ is highly relevant because dysfunction in adipokine signaling is a major feature of obesity-associated diabetes, and adiponectin is widely regarded as a protective endocrine factor in this disease setting.

In a related but distinct way, ADM appears relevant to diabetes primarily through its vascular and metabolic implications. Although the provided function emphasizes receptor usage rather than a specific diabetic phenotype, adrenomedullin signaling is notable because diabetes is characterized not only by disordered glucose metabolism but also by endothelial dysfunction, altered tissue perfusion, and progressive microvascular injury. A ligand with defined activity through calcitonin receptor-like receptor and receptor activity-modifying protein receptor complexes may influence vascular tone, endothelial integrity, and tissue stress responses, all of which are highly pertinent to diabetic complications such as nephropathy, retinopathy, and cardiovascular disease. ADM therefore stands out as a potential mediator at the interface between metabolic disease and vascular adaptation. Its importance may be greater in the complication phase of diabetes than in primary insulin resistance, but this still makes it biologically meaningful across the broader diabetic disease spectrum.

Extending from vascular adaptation to extracellular remodeling, PLAUR is of interest in diabetes because it connects extracellular proteolysis, cell-surface signaling, and tissue remodeling, processes that are frequently dysregulated in chronic diabetic states. Its role in localizing urokinase activity and promoting plasmin formation suggests involvement in matrix turnover, inflammatory cell migration, and wound repair. These functions are especially relevant to diabetes, where impaired tissue remodeling and defective healing are common clinical problems, particularly in the skin, vasculature, and kidney. In addition, the proteolysis-independent signaling functions of PLAUR imply that it may influence inflammatory or stress-response pathways beyond matrix degradation alone. This is important because diabetes is increasingly understood as a disease of both metabolic dysfunction and maladaptive inflammation. Thus, PLAUR may be mechanistically linked to diabetic complications through altered extracellular matrix dynamics, inflammation, and repair processes.[PubMed:15677461](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15677461) 

Finally, LAMB1 is less directly connected to core glucose homeostasis than ADIPOQ, but it remains potentially relevant to diabetes because basement membrane structure and extracellular matrix organization are central to diabetic tissue injury. The described role of LAMB1 in cell attachment, migration, and maintenance of basement membrane integrity suggests a broader importance in preserving tissue architecture. In diabetes, excessive extracellular matrix remodeling and basement membrane thickening are hallmark features of microvascular complications, particularly in the kidney and retina. A laminin subunit involved in structural organization may therefore contribute to susceptibility or response to diabetic damage, even if the provided functional description is framed mainly in developmental and neuroarchitectural terms. Its relevance is thus likely indirect but still meaningful, especially in relation to chronic tissue remodeling and barrier dysfunction in diabetic complications.

### Duodenum; endocrine cells[≥Low] (HPA:0151291) 

The pathway described as duodenum endocrine cells with low or greater expression refers to the population of hormone-secreting enteroendocrine cells located in the proximal small intestine, especially within the duodenal mucosa. These cells act as nutrient sensors and convert luminal exposure to carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, bile acids, and microbial metabolites into endocrine, paracrine, and neurohumoral signals that regulate gastric emptying, pancreatic secretion, insulin release, glucagon regulation, appetite, intestinal motility, and systemic glucose homeostasis. Major functional outputs of duodenal endocrine cells include secretion of glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon-like peptide one, serotonin, cholecystokinin, secretin, and other peptide mediators. Although this pathway is anatomically centered in the intestine rather than the pancreatic islet, it appears highly relevant to diabetes because it lies upstream of insulin secretion, incretin responsiveness, nutrient handling, and gut-immune communication. Recent work further indicates that duodenal epithelial programs are altered in type one diabetes, with increased enteroendocrine cell representation and broader disturbances in epithelial differentiation, proliferation, barrier function, and ion transport, suggesting that the diabetic state may involve remodeling of the proximal intestinal endocrine compartment rather than only pancreatic pathology. In obesity and type two diabetes, the duodenum is increasingly viewed as an active endocrine organ whose cellular composition and meal-stimulated signaling may become maladaptive, thereby contributing to impaired glycemic regulation.

Building on this physiological framework, the collected literature indicates that duodenal endocrine cells are related to diabetes through at least three interconnected mechanisms: incretin and anti-incretin regulation of insulin secretion, intestinal remodeling in metabolic disease, and gut-derived immune or neurohormonal signaling that influences endocrine homeostasis. A central theme is that the duodenum is a major source of glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide and other nutrient-responsive hormones that shape postprandial insulin release and whole-body glucose control; accordingly, duodenal enteroendocrine cells and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide have been proposed as therapeutic targets in obesity and type two diabetes, particularly because interventions that reduce nutrient contact with the duodenal mucosa improve glycemic control and body weight while enhancing more distal glucagon-like peptide one signaling, as seen after bariatric procedures and with dual receptor agonist therapy such as tirzepatide (PubMed:38320643). Consistent with disease-linked remodeling of this compartment, duodenal biopsies from individuals with obesity showed increased chromogranin A-positive, glucagon-like peptide one-positive, and serotonin-positive endocrine cells, and glucagon-like peptide one cell abundance correlated with glycated hemoglobin and meal-test glucose, implying that increased endocrine cell number may reflect compensation for insufficient incretin action rather than effective metabolic control (PubMed:40790227). Experimental work also suggests that direct duodenal ablation can improve insulin sensitivity and alter meal-stimulated incretin profiles, supporting a possible causal role for abnormal proximal intestinal signaling in dysglycemia (PubMed:37778055). In parallel, a mechanistic review advanced the concept that chronic overstimulation of proximal intestinal endocrine cells, particularly cholecystokinin-producing and secretin-producing cells, may generate excessive neurohormonal signals that promote insulin resistance and progressive beta-cell failure, thereby placing the duodenum upstream of type two diabetes pathogenesis, although this model remains exploratory (PubMed:40864811). The relevance of this pathway is not limited to type two diabetes. In pediatric type one diabetes, duodenal enteroid studies demonstrated altered epithelial differentiation, increased enteroendocrine cell expression, impaired barrier integrity, and abnormal secretory physiology, indicating that the proximal intestinal endocrine niche is structurally and functionally remodeled in autoimmune diabetes as well (PubMed:38789719). More broadly, gut-endocrine and immune communication appears capable of influencing distant pancreatic endocrine protection, as gut microbiota-conditioned innate lymphoid cells were shown to induce an interleukin twenty-two-dependent protective program in pancreatic endocrine cells that prevents autoimmune diabetes in mice, demonstrating that intestinal signals can regulate endocrine survival beyond the gut itself (PubMed:30017352). Taken together, these studies support the interpretation that the duodenal endocrine cell pathway is closely linked to diabetes because it integrates nutrient sensing, incretin biology, mucosal adaptation, and gut-derived immune and neurohormonal signals that collectively modulate insulin secretion, glucagon balance, insulin sensitivity, and progression of both autoimmune and metabolic forms of diabetes.[PubMed:38320643](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38320643) [PubMed:40790227](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40790227) [PubMed:37778055](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37778055) [PubMed:40864811](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40864811) [PubMed:38789719](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38789719) [PubMed:30017352](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30017352) 

Against this biological background, the enrichment results provide a quantitative indication that this intestinal endocrine program may capture a substantial fraction of diabetes-relevant molecular activity. There were 74 diabetes-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway described as duodenum endocrine cells with low or greater expression, indicating a substantial functional concentration of disease-linked proteins within an intestinal endocrine program that is highly relevant to systemic glucose regulation, insulin secretion, glucagon control, nutrient sensing, gastrointestinal motility, and enteroinsular communication. This protein count of 74 supports the interpretation that diabetes biology extends beyond pancreatic tissue alone and includes a quantitatively notable remodeling of the proximal intestinal endocrine compartment, particularly because this pathway captures hormone-secreting epithelial cells that integrate luminal nutrient exposure into endocrine and paracrine outputs with direct consequences for glycemic homeostasis.

To place these 74 proteins into a systems-level context, the network representation below summarizes their protein-protein interaction structure and provides a basis for examining how these diabetes-associated components may be functionally connected.

The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network of these 74 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network exploration and evidence review.

![PPI Network](imgs/35d1cb45-b65f-486d-bae3-041a190404e2.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=E23D4EC851E65737)

With this network context in mind, the function enrichment analysis identified several significant proteins that may help explain how this pathway connects intestinal endocrine biology with broader metabolic and inflammatory processes relevant to diabetes. We introduce them in detail below.

FBP1 is among the most directly relevant proteins in this list for diabetes because it occupies a central position in hepatic glucose production, a core pathogenic process in type two diabetes. Excessive gluconeogenesis is a major contributor to fasting hyperglycemia, and FBP1, as a rate-limiting gluconeogenic enzyme, is therefore mechanistically linked to impaired glycemic control. Its additional effects on pancreatic beta-cell glucose sensing and insulin secretion further increase its relevance, since diabetes reflects not only increased hepatic glucose output but also defective endocrine regulation. The reported association with appetite and adiposity suggests that FBP1 may also participate in broader metabolic feedback loops that influence obesity, insulin resistance, and energy balance, all of which are major determinants of diabetes risk and progression.

In a related metabolic direction, KHK highlights the potential contribution of dietary substrate handling to diabetes-associated dysfunction. KHK is highly relevant to diabetes because fructose metabolism has been strongly implicated in metabolic syndrome, hepatic steatosis, insulin resistance, and type two diabetes. By catalyzing the first committed step in fructose utilization, KHK enables rapid hepatic fructose flux, which can promote lipogenesis, adenosine triphosphate depletion, uric acid generation, and downstream metabolic stress. These processes are closely connected to obesity-associated insulin resistance and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, which frequently co-occur with diabetes. Although the annotation here is concise, the biological role of KHK places it at an important intersection between dietary sugar exposure and metabolic dysfunction.

Extending this theme of intermediary metabolism, GPD1 points to altered substrate partitioning between carbohydrate and lipid pathways. GPD1 is metabolically important in diabetes because glycerol-3-phosphate metabolism links carbohydrate handling, triglyceride synthesis, and redox balance. Through its enzymatic activity, GPD1 contributes to the conversion of glycerol-derived intermediates that can support hepatic gluconeogenesis and lipid accumulation. In the diabetic state, dysregulated glycerol flux from adipose lipolysis feeds hepatic glucose production and triglyceride synthesis, thereby exacerbating hyperglycemia and steatosis. Even though the functional annotation is brief, the enzyme's placement in intermediary metabolism makes it relevant to the altered substrate partitioning characteristic of insulin resistance.

A complementary aspect of this metabolic dysregulation is reflected by CES1, which may connect adipose lipid mobilization with systemic insulin sensitivity. CES1 stands out because adipose tissue lipolysis is a major determinant of systemic insulin sensitivity. As a major lipase in white adipose tissue, CES1 may influence the release of fatty acids and glycerol into the circulation, thereby affecting ectopic lipid deposition, hepatic gluconeogenesis, and peripheral insulin resistance. Increased fatty acid flux from adipose tissue is a well-established driver of metabolic dysfunction in type two diabetes. The ability of CES1 to act on retinyl esters may also be relevant, since retinoid metabolism can modulate adipocyte biology and glucose homeostasis. Thus, CES1 connects lipid mobilization with metabolic stress pathways central to diabetes pathogenesis.[PubMed:15220344](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15220344) 

Consistent with the importance of intestinal and hepatic lipid handling, APOA4 may provide an additional link between postprandial nutrient processing and diabetic metabolic imbalance. APOA4 is relevant to diabetes because diabetic dyslipidemia is a major feature of insulin-resistant states and an important contributor to cardiovascular risk. By participating in chylomicron and very low-density lipoprotein metabolism and supporting lipoprotein lipase activation, APOA4 may influence postprandial lipid clearance, triglyceride handling, and high-density lipoprotein function. These pathways are frequently disrupted in type two diabetes, where impaired lipoprotein metabolism contributes to both metabolic deterioration and vascular complications. APOA4 therefore stands out as a candidate linking intestinal lipid transport and systemic metabolic homeostasis.

Along similar lines, FABP1 may reflect the hepatic intracellular consequences of excess lipid exposure. FABP1 is important in the context of diabetes because the liver is a central organ in insulin resistance, lipid overload, and glucose overproduction. By binding and trafficking fatty acids and related lipids within hepatocytes, FABP1 may influence beta-oxidation, lipid storage, and lipotoxic stress. Hepatic lipid accumulation is tightly linked to impaired insulin signaling and increased gluconeogenesis, both hallmarks of type two diabetes. FABP1 may therefore contribute to the interface between altered lipid handling and dysregulated glucose metabolism, especially in individuals with fatty liver disease.

Beyond core metabolism, the enriched set also includes proteins that may be relevant to vascular homeostasis and diabetes-related complications. DDAH1 is particularly relevant to diabetes complications because nitric oxide bioavailability is a critical determinant of endothelial function, vascular tone, and tissue perfusion. In diabetes, elevated asymmetric dimethylarginine and impaired nitric oxide signaling contribute to endothelial dysfunction, hypertension, nephropathy, and macrovascular disease. By degrading asymmetric dimethylarginine and monomethylarginine, DDAH1 may preserve nitric oxide production and protect against vascular injury. This places DDAH1 at the center of mechanisms linking metabolic disease to cardiovascular and microvascular complications, which are major causes of morbidity in diabetes.

In a related inflammatory and tissue-protective context, CFI suggests a possible role for complement regulation in diabetes-associated injury. CFI is relevant because chronic low-grade inflammation and innate immune activation are increasingly recognized as contributors to insulin resistance and diabetic tissue injury. Complement dysregulation has been implicated in vascular inflammation, renal damage, and metabolic dysfunction. By inactivating C3b and C4b, CFI restrains complement amplification and helps protect healthy host tissues from inflammatory injury. This function may be especially important in diabetes, where endothelial surfaces, glomeruli, and other metabolically stressed tissues are vulnerable to inflammatory damage. Thus, CFI may have particular significance for diabetic nephropathy and vascular complications.[PubMed:17320177](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17320177) [PubMed:7360115](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7360115) [PubMed:12055245](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12055245) [PubMed:2141838](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2141838) [PubMed:9605165](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9605165) [PubMed:28671664](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28671664) 

This inflammatory dimension becomes even more apparent with IL18, which may connect innate immune activation to metabolic dysfunction. IL18 is one of the strongest inflammation-related candidates in this list for diabetes relevance. Chronic metaflammation is a defining feature of obesity-associated insulin resistance and type two diabetes, and IL18 participates in innate and adaptive immune signaling through nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation and T helper one and natural killer cell responses. Its release downstream of pyroptosis is especially notable, as inflammasome activation and pyroptotic signaling have been implicated in adipose inflammation, beta-cell stress, and diabetic complications. IL18 may therefore contribute both to systemic insulin resistance and to local inflammatory damage in metabolic tissues.[PubMed:26638072](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26638072) [PubMed:26638073](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26638073) [PubMed:30392956](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30392956) 

Closely aligned with this observation, GCHFR may point to a more specific inflammasome-related mechanism. GCHFR is highly interesting from the perspective of diabetes-related inflammation because it is directly linked to non-canonical NLRP3 inflammasome activation. The NLRP3 inflammasome has been widely implicated in obesity-induced inflammation, insulin resistance, pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction, and diabetic complications. By promoting the association of NLRP3 with NEK7 in response to inflammatory danger signals, GCHFR may amplify pyroptotic and cytokine-driven pathways that worsen metabolic homeostasis. This makes it a potentially important mediator connecting innate immune sensing to diabetes pathogenesis.

In addition to inflammatory stress, proteostatic stress appears repeatedly across the enriched proteins, with ERN1 representing a prominent example. ERN1 (IRE1) is a major mechanistic link between cellular stress and diabetes. Endoplasmic reticulum stress is a well-established contributor to insulin resistance, beta-cell dysfunction, and lipotoxicity in obesity and type two diabetes. By sensing misfolded proteins and activating the XBP1 arm of the unfolded protein response, ERN1 governs adaptive and maladaptive responses to secretory and metabolic stress. In pancreatic beta-cells, which have an exceptionally high protein-folding burden due to insulin biosynthesis, dysregulated ERN1 signaling can influence survival and secretory capacity. In liver and adipose tissue, chronic unfolded protein response activation also contributes to inflammation and impaired insulin action.[PubMed:11175748](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11175748) [PubMed:11779464](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11779464) [PubMed:12637535](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12637535) [PubMed:21317875](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21317875) [PubMed:28128204](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28128204) [PubMed:30118681](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30118681) [PubMed:9637683](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9637683) [PubMed:19328063](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19328063) [PubMed:24508390](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24508390) [PubMed:21884936](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21884936) [PubMed:28067262](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28067262) 

Following this same endoplasmic reticulum-centered perspective, ENTPD5 may further reflect the importance of protein maturation capacity in metabolically stressed secretory cells. ENTPD5 is relevant to diabetes because efficient endoplasmic reticulum protein folding is essential for the biosynthesis and maturation of secreted and membrane proteins, including those involved in insulin production and metabolic signaling. By clearing uridine diphosphate from the endoplasmic reticulum lumen and supporting glycoprotein reglucosylation, ENTPD5 enhances protein quality control. This function is particularly important in highly secretory cells such as pancreatic beta-cells, where endoplasmic reticulum stress and defective proteostasis are central to diabetes pathogenesis. ENTPD5 may therefore influence beta-cell resilience and the maintenance of insulin secretory function under metabolic stress.[PubMed:10369669](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10369669) [PubMed:21074248](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21074248) 

P4HB extends this proteostasis theme by emphasizing oxidative folding and chaperone activity. P4HB is important in diabetes because oxidative protein folding and chaperone-mediated proteostasis are central to pancreatic beta-cell function. Insulin biosynthesis requires correct disulfide bond formation, and disturbances in endoplasmic reticulum folding capacity can trigger stress responses, impair insulin maturation, and promote beta-cell failure. The multifunctional role of P4HB in disulfide exchange and chaperoning therefore makes it a plausible contributor to beta-cell vulnerability in diabetes. In addition, its cell-surface redox activity may have broader implications for inflammatory and vascular responses in diabetic tissues.[PubMed:21670307](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21670307) 

At the membrane level, altered lipid composition may also shape diabetes-related cell dysfunction, which brings PCYT2 into focus. PCYT2 is relevant to diabetes because phospholipid composition strongly influences membrane integrity, organelle function, insulin signaling, and lipid metabolism. Phosphatidylethanolamine is a major inner-leaflet membrane phospholipid and is important for membrane protein stability, cell division, apoptosis, and cellular stress responses. Altered phospholipid metabolism has been associated with insulin resistance, mitochondrial dysfunction, and hepatic steatosis. By controlling phosphatidylethanolamine synthesis, PCYT2 may therefore affect metabolic flexibility and cellular resilience in tissues central to diabetes pathophysiology.[PubMed:31637422](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31637422) [PubMed:9083101](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9083101) 

A related organelle-level perspective is provided by PLSCR3, which may connect membrane remodeling with mitochondrial performance. PLSCR3 stands out because mitochondrial dysfunction is a fundamental feature of insulin resistance and diabetic tissue injury. By regulating cardiolipin distribution, mitochondrial morphology, and apoptotic susceptibility, PLSCR3 may influence oxidative metabolism and cell survival. In metabolic tissues such as liver, muscle, adipose tissue, and pancreatic beta-cells, impaired mitochondrial function can contribute to defective insulin action, altered substrate oxidation, and increased cell death. The connection of PLSCR3 to cardiolipin remodeling is particularly notable, as cardiolipin is essential for mitochondrial bioenergetics and stress responses.

Shifting from intracellular organelles to insulin-responsive trafficking, PTPRM may be especially pertinent to glucose disposal. PTPRM is especially relevant to diabetes because it is directly connected to GLUT4 (SLC2A4) membrane trafficking, a central determinant of insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in adipose tissue and muscle. By modulating CTNND1 phosphorylation and allowing SLC2A4 to reach the plasma membrane, PTPRM may support effective glucose disposal. Defects in GLUT4 trafficking are a hallmark of insulin resistance, and proteins that influence this process are highly pertinent to type two diabetes. Its role in adipogenic differentiation further suggests broader effects on adipose tissue biology and systemic metabolic homeostasis.[PubMed:10753936](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10753936) [PubMed:17761881](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17761881) [PubMed:21998202](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21998202) 

In parallel, signaling pathways involved in tissue remodeling and vascular adaptation may also contribute to the broader disease spectrum, as illustrated by NOTCH1. NOTCH1 is relevant to diabetes because Notch signaling influences tissue remodeling, vascular biology, and cell differentiation in ways that intersect with diabetic complications and metabolic dysfunction. Its anti-angiogenic effects in endothelial cells are particularly notable, as aberrant angiogenesis and endothelial dysfunction are central to diabetic retinopathy, nephropathy, and impaired wound healing. More broadly, Notch signaling has been implicated in pancreatic development, fibrosis, and inflammatory remodeling. Although not a classic metabolic enzyme, NOTCH1 stands out as a signaling hub with potential importance in both diabetes progression and complication biology.

This vascular and remodeling perspective is further supported by COL18A1, which may influence pathological angiogenesis. COL18A1 is of interest in diabetes primarily because vascular remodeling and pathological angiogenesis are central features of diabetic complications, especially retinopathy. Its anti-angiogenic activity, including inhibition of vascular endothelial growth factor A-mediated endothelial proliferation and migration, suggests a plausible role in modulating abnormal neovascular responses. Since excessive vascular endothelial growth factor signaling contributes to diabetic microvascular disease, proteins such as COL18A1 may influence the severity or progression of vascular complications. This makes COL18A1 more relevant to complication mechanisms than to primary glucose dysregulation, but still highly important in the broader diabetic disease spectrum.[PubMed:9459295](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9459295) [PubMed:11257123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257123) 

Finally, several enriched proteins point toward retinoid and lipid mediator biology as additional, although somewhat less direct, modulators of diabetes-related phenotypes. ADH1B is noteworthy because retinoid metabolism is increasingly recognized as a regulator of adipogenesis, insulin sensitivity, hepatic metabolism, and beta-cell biology. By participating in retinol and retinal interconversion, ADH1B may influence the generation of bioactive retinoid signals that affect metabolic gene expression. Although its connection to diabetes is less direct than that of gluconeogenic or inflammatory proteins, altered retinoid homeostasis has been linked to obesity, fatty liver, and insulin resistance, making ADH1B a potentially relevant metabolic modifier.[PubMed:15369820](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15369820) [PubMed:16787387](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16787387) 

Within this same general biochemical space, ADH4 may connect retinoid turnover with vascular and renal injury pathways. ADH4 is relevant to diabetes through two complementary mechanisms: retinoid metabolism and lipid mediator metabolism. Retinoids influence adipocyte differentiation, insulin action, and hepatic metabolism, while 20-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid and related eicosanoids are implicated in vascular tone, inflammation, and renal injury. Because diabetic complications often involve both metabolic dysregulation and vascular damage, ADH4 may contribute to disease processes at the interface of lipid signaling and tissue injury. Its role in oxidizing omega-hydroxy fatty acids may be particularly pertinent to diabetic nephropathy and vascular dysfunction.[PubMed:17279314](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17279314) [PubMed:16081420](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16081420) 

Extending this tentative retinoid-related interpretation, GPRC5C emerges as a more hypothesis-generating candidate. GPRC5C is an interesting candidate because it may connect retinoid signaling to broader receptor-mediated pathways that regulate metabolism. Retinoic acid signaling has known effects on glucose homeostasis, adipogenesis, and hepatic lipid handling. Although the functional annotation is limited, a retinoic acid-inducible G protein-coupled receptor could plausibly participate in nutrient-responsive signaling networks relevant to insulin sensitivity and metabolic adaptation. Its significance is therefore more hypothesis-generating than established, but it stands out due to the importance of retinoid pathways in metabolic disease.

### regulation of vasculature development (GO:1901342) 

Regulation of vasculature development comprises all biological processes that increase, decrease, or otherwise shape the formation, patterning, maturation, and remodeling of blood vessels. This pathway includes endothelial cell proliferation, migration, sprouting, branching morphogenesis, lumen formation, recruitment of mural cells, stabilization of newly formed vessels, and tissue-specific angiocrine signaling that coordinates organ growth and metabolic function. Proper regulation is essential because both insufficient and excessive vessel formation can impair tissue oxygenation, nutrient delivery, endocrine exchange, and barrier integrity. In metabolic organs, especially pancreatic islets, retina, bone, placenta, heart, and brain, vascular development is not merely structural but also instructive, because developing vessels provide signals that influence cell differentiation, secretory capacity, and tissue homeostasis. The publications provided indicate that this pathway is governed by factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor A, hypoxia inducible factor signaling, endothelin one, adrenomedullin, renin angiotensin signaling, endothelial sirtuin pathways, and tissue-specific endothelial or paracrine regulators. In the context of diabetes, regulation of vasculature development spans early developmental programming, adaptive or maladaptive vascular remodeling during obesity and insulin resistance, and progressive microvascular injury that underlies complications such as diabetic retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, impaired wound healing, cognitive decline, placental dysfunction, and diabetic bone disease.  

Against this biological background, the collected literature suggests that regulation of vasculature development is closely intertwined with diabetes at both causal and consequence levels. First, altered vascular developmental programs can directly shape later glucose homeostasis. In pancreatic islets, beta two adrenergic receptor signaling restrains vascular endothelial growth factor A production during neonatal development; loss of this control causes excessive islet vascularization, defective insulin secretion, and adult glucose intolerance, suggesting that abnormal vessel growth during organogenesis can predispose to diabetes-relevant endocrine dysfunction (PubMed:30303066). Consistently, reviews on islet biology and transplantation emphasize that endothelial cells and islet vasculature are indispensable for endocrine maturation, survival, and function, further linking vascular developmental regulation to diabetes pathogenesis and therapy (PubMed:40330424, PubMed:34589059). Second, diabetes and obesity actively reprogram endothelial signaling pathways that control vascular remodeling. A particularly strong mechanistic study shows that endothelial FUN14 domain containing one is increased under diabetic conditions and promotes the obesity to type two diabetes transition through sirtuin three, GATA binding protein two, and endothelin one signaling, identifying the vascular endothelium as a potential driver of systemic metabolic deterioration rather than merely a passive target (PubMed:41545370). More broadly, diabetes is characterized by endothelial dysfunction, impaired nitric oxide bioavailability, oxidative stress, inflammation, and disturbed angiogenesis, all of which alter the frequency, rate, and quality of vessel growth and remodeling across tissues (PubMed:22577553, PubMed:39767191, PubMed:40032212). Third, dysregulated vascular development and remodeling contribute centrally to diabetic complications. In the retina, diabetes disrupts neurovascular regulation, promotes early vascular compromise, and ultimately drives capillary degeneration and pathological angiogenesis; protective roles for sirtuin one and microglial vascular regulation further indicate that altered control of vessel maintenance and remodeling is a key determinant of diabetic retinopathy progression (PubMed:29311218, PubMed:40020909, PubMed:35574010). In the brain, type two diabetes is linked to defective neurovascular coupling and microvascular pericyte pathology, providing a vascular developmental and remodeling framework for diabetes-associated cognitive decline and its overlap with neurodegeneration (PubMed:35860697, PubMed:39222475). In bone, type two diabetes related osteoporosis is associated with loss of specialized H type vessels, and restoration of Elabela apelin receptor signaling rescues angiogenesis osteogenesis coupling, indicating that diabetes may impair tissue specific vascular niche development with functional skeletal consequences (PubMed:41455365). Developmental exposure is also important: maternal diabetes perturbs cardiovascular and coronary vascular development in offspring, and gestational diabetes alters placental angiogenesis and vascular function, showing that diabetic environments can dysregulate vasculature development before birth with lasting effects on fetal oxygenation and cardiovascular risk (PubMed:38505753, PubMed:33453370). Finally, circulating vasoactive mediators such as adrenomedullin are elevated in diabetes and correlate with complications, supporting the concept that persistent diabetic metabolic stress shifts vascular growth and homeostatic signaling toward maladaptive remodeling (PubMed:24936257). Taken together, the evidence indicates that regulation of vasculature development is not peripheral to diabetes; rather, it appears to represent a core axis linking developmental programming, endothelial metabolic signaling, tissue specific vascular niche integrity, and the emergence of both systemic metabolic dysfunction and chronic diabetic complications.[PubMed:30303066](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30303066) [PubMed:40330424](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40330424) [PubMed:34589059](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34589059) [PubMed:41545370](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41545370) [PubMed:22577553](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22577553) [PubMed:39767191](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39767191) [PubMed:40032212](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40032212) [PubMed:29311218](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29311218) [PubMed:40020909](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40020909) [PubMed:35574010](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35574010) [PubMed:35860697](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35860697) [PubMed:39222475](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39222475) [PubMed:41455365](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41455365) [PubMed:38505753](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38505753) [PubMed:33453370](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33453370) [PubMed:24936257](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24936257) 

There were 50 diabetes-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of regulation of vasculature development, a biological program that governs the formation, patterning, maturation, and remodeling of blood vessels and is highly relevant to diabetes because vascular dysregulation contributes directly to metabolic dysfunction and to complications affecting the retina, kidney, nerve, heart, brain, placenta, bone, and wound repair. This enrichment across 50 proteins indicates a substantial concentration of diabetes-related molecular signals within vascular developmental control, consistent with the central role of endothelial proliferation, migration, sprouting, branching, lumen formation, mural cell recruitment, vessel stabilization, and tissue-specific angiocrine communication in diabetic pathophysiology.  

To place these enriched proteins into a systems-level context, the network representation below illustrates their interaction structure and connectivity.

The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network of these 50 proteins, together with the link to the STRING webpage for interactive inspection of the network topology and connectivity relationships.

![PPI Network](imgs/36518e48-d846-448d-a87e-cbb3e6bb0773.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=44C8388C7847B339)

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  
With that overall network context in place, the following paragraphs summarize the proteins that appear especially notable within this enriched set and discuss their possible relevance to diabetes in a cautious, evidence-based manner.

DLL1 is among the most diabetes-relevant proteins in this list because Notch signaling is fundamentally involved in pancreatic lineage specification and endocrine cell differentiation. The reported role of DLL1 in maintaining pancreatic progenitors and regulating early pancreatic epithelial patterning suggests a direct connection to beta-cell developmental competence and, by extension, long-term insulin secretory capacity. Beyond organogenesis, DLL1 also contributes to arterial identity and endothelial responsiveness to vascular endothelial growth factor A, linking it to vascular homeostasis. This is particularly important in diabetes, where both impaired beta-cell mass and microvascular dysfunction are central pathogenic features. Dysregulated DLL1-Notch signaling could therefore plausibly contribute both to defective pancreatic cell differentiation and to diabetic vascular complications through altered endothelial behavior and angiogenic control.[PubMed:11006133](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11006133) [PubMed:11581320](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11581320)  

Building on this developmental theme, HHEX stands out because it is a well-established diabetes susceptibility locus in human genetics, and the functional description provided here is highly consistent with that association. Its ability to regulate developmental signaling pathways, particularly WNT and NODAL, indicates a role in early endodermal and pancreatic patterning programs that are essential for proper islet formation. Since diabetes can arise from impaired beta-cell development, reduced functional beta-cell mass, or altered endocrine lineage maintenance, a transcription factor such as HHEX is mechanistically relevant even when its role is indirect. The reported interaction with CTNNB1-dependent transcription further strengthens the connection, as WNT signaling influences pancreatic progenitor biology and metabolic tissue differentiation. Thus, HHEX is important as a developmental regulator whose perturbation could predispose to beta-cell insufficiency and diabetes susceptibility.[PubMed:20028982](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20028982) [PubMed:12554669](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12554669) [PubMed:8096636](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8096636)  

Whereas DLL1 and HHEX point primarily to developmental specification, PTPRM is highly relevant to diabetes because its annotated function directly intersects with insulin-responsive glucose transport. The protein promotes plasma membrane trafficking of solute carrier family two member four, also known as glucose transporter type four, the principal insulin-regulated glucose transporter in adipose tissue and muscle. Impaired glucose transporter type four translocation is a core molecular defect in insulin resistance and type two diabetes. In this context, PTPRM may influence systemic glucose disposal by modulating adipocyte differentiation and preserving efficient glucose uptake machinery. Its effects on cell-cell adhesion and catenin phosphorylation also suggest broader roles in adipose tissue architecture and metabolic signaling. Among the proteins listed, PTPRM is especially notable because the mechanistic link to diabetes is immediate and centered on one of the defining biochemical abnormalities of the disease: defective peripheral glucose uptake.[PubMed:10753936](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10753936) [PubMed:17761881](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17761881) [PubMed:21998202](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21998202)  

Extending from glucose transport to endothelial regulation, AMOT is of particular interest in diabetes because it integrates endothelial barrier function with Hippo and yes associated protein one signaling, two processes increasingly implicated in diabetic complications and metabolic tissue remodeling. Diabetes is characterized by chronic endothelial dysfunction, altered vascular permeability, and abnormal angiogenic responses, especially in the retina, kidney, and wound microenvironment. AMOT may influence these processes by controlling tight junction stability and endothelial migration. Its repression of yes associated protein one and tafazzin is also noteworthy, since this signaling affects cell survival, regeneration, fibrosis, and potentially beta-cell adaptive responses. Therefore, AMOT may be relevant not only to diabetic microvascular disease but also to tissue remodeling in organs exposed to glucotoxicity and inflammation.[PubMed:21205866](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21205866)  

A related aspect of vascular remodeling involves extracellular matrix turnover, which makes CEMIP2 relevant to diabetes because extracellular matrix remodeling and hyaluronan turnover are increasingly recognized as contributors to insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, impaired wound healing, and diabetic cardiovascular disease. Hyaluronan accumulation is frequently observed in inflamed and fibrotic tissues, including adipose tissue and diabetic wounds, where it alters leukocyte recruitment, tissue stiffness, and repair responses. By degrading high-molecular-weight hyaluronan and influencing focal adhesion dynamics, CEMIP2 may shape cell migration and angiogenesis in metabolically stressed tissues. Its reported connection to vascular endothelial growth factor signaling further supports a role in diabetic vascular pathology, where abnormal angiogenesis and matrix remodeling are central features.[PubMed:28246172](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28246172) [PubMed:37196767](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37196767) [PubMed:37527776](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37527776) [PubMed:33647313](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33647313) [PubMed:34624311](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34624311)  

In parallel with matrix remodeling, inflammatory regulation is also likely to be important, and CHI3L1 is notable because it links inflammation, macrophage polarization, epithelial stress responses, and tissue remodeling, all of which are highly relevant to diabetes pathogenesis and its complications. Chronic low-grade inflammation is a hallmark of insulin resistance, and macrophage functional states in adipose tissue strongly influence metabolic homeostasis. The ability of CHI3L1 to promote M2 macrophage differentiation, modulate dendritic cell accumulation, and activate protein kinase B one and interleukin eight signaling suggests that it could shape inflammatory microenvironments in obesity, diabetic wounds, and end-organ injury. In addition, its role in tissue remodeling may connect it to fibrosis and extracellular matrix changes observed in diabetic nephropathy and other chronic complications. Thus, CHI3L1 is important primarily as an immunometabolic and remodeling-associated mediator.  

Consistent with this vascular-inflammatory interface, GDF2 is highly pertinent to diabetes because vascular integrity and endothelial signaling are central determinants of diabetic complications. The protein regulates angiogenesis and vessel stability and signals through the bone morphogenetic protein and transforming growth factor beta axis, pathways that are strongly implicated in endothelial homeostasis, inflammation, and fibrosis. In diabetes, persistent hyperglycemia disrupts endothelial function and promotes both excessive and insufficient angiogenesis depending on tissue context, such as proliferative retinopathy versus impaired wound repair. Because GDF2 supports normal vascular structure and modulates mothers against decapentaplegic homolog signaling, altered GDF2 activity could contribute to the vascular fragility, maladaptive remodeling, and organ-specific microangiopathy that define advanced diabetic disease.[PubMed:10625534](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10625534) [PubMed:17540773](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17540773) [PubMed:28530658](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28530658) [PubMed:23300529](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23300529)  

Along similar lines, HRG stands out because it sits at the intersection of inflammation, coagulation, endothelial signaling, and angiogenesis, all of which are profoundly altered in diabetes. Diabetic vasculopathy is characterized not only by endothelial dysfunction but also by a prothrombotic state, chronic sterile inflammation, and impaired resolution of tissue injury. HRG can modulate necrotic cell clearance, vascular endothelial growth factor signaling, macrophage polarization, and endothelial motility, suggesting potential relevance to diabetic wound healing, atherosclerosis, nephropathy, and retinopathy. Its heparan sulfate-dependent interactions are also notable because the endothelial glycocalyx is disrupted in diabetes. Accordingly, HRG may influence both vascular injury responses and inflammatory homeostasis in diabetic tissues.  

This convergence of inflammation and repair is also reflected in MDK, which is one of the most compelling proteins in this list for diabetes-related biology because it combines pro-inflammatory, pro-survival, pro-angiogenic, and tissue-repair functions. Diabetes involves chronic inflammation together with defective regenerative responses, especially in the vasculature, kidney, peripheral nerves, and skin. MDK recruits inflammatory cells, influences dendritic cell and T-cell responses, and activates mitogen-activated protein kinase and protein kinase B signaling, all of which could contribute to metabolic inflammation. At the same time, its ability to induce vascular endothelial growth factor A, promote endothelial proliferation, and support tissue regeneration links it to diabetic wound healing and vascular remodeling. This dual role is particularly relevant in diabetes, where excessive inflammation coexists with inadequate repair. MDK may therefore act as a context-dependent mediator of both compensatory regeneration and pathological remodeling.[PubMed:10212223](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [PubMed:10683378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [PubMed:10772929](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [PubMed:12084985](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [PubMed:12122009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [PubMed:12573468](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12573468) [PubMed:15466886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [PubMed:18469519](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [PubMed:22323540](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [PubMed:24458438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438)  

At the center of several of these observations is vascular endothelial growth factor-driven endothelial signaling. Regardless of the apparent annotation inconsistency in the source description, the listed functions clearly correspond to a central vascular endothelial growth factor-driven endothelial signaling axis that is highly relevant to diabetes. Diabetes-associated complications are fundamentally vascular, involving altered permeability, aberrant angiogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, and impaired nitric oxide bioavailability. A protein controlling vascular endothelial growth factor-dependent endothelial migration, survival, cytoskeletal remodeling, and nitric oxide signaling would therefore be directly implicated in diabetic retinopathy, nephropathy, macrovascular disease, and poor wound healing. This entry is especially important because it captures the convergence of vascular endothelial growth factor signaling and endothelial nitric oxide pathways, both of which are repeatedly dysregulated in hyperglycemic states.  

In a related anti-angiogenic context, SERPINF1 is particularly relevant to diabetes because anti-angiogenic balance is a major determinant of diabetic microvascular disease, especially retinopathy. A potent endogenous inhibitor of angiogenesis could modulate pathological neovascularization, which is a defining feature of proliferative diabetic retinopathy. Its neurotrophic activity is also noteworthy because diabetic neuropathy involves both vascular and neuronal injury. Therefore, SERPINF1 may be important at the interface of neurovascular protection, potentially influencing retinal integrity, peripheral nerve health, and tissue responses to chronic metabolic stress.  

Beyond angiogenic balance alone, developmental signaling pathways may also intersect with diabetic remodeling, and SFRP1 is relevant to diabetes because Wnt signaling is increasingly implicated in adipogenesis, insulin sensitivity, pancreatic development, fibrosis, and vascular remodeling. By antagonizing beta-catenin-dependent signaling, SFRP1 may influence adipose tissue expansion and differentiation, processes tightly linked to systemic insulin resistance. Its effects on vascular cell proliferation and angiogenesis further connect it to diabetic vasculopathy. In addition, Wnt pathway dysregulation has been associated with beta-cell dysfunction and diabetic kidney disease, making SFRP1 a plausible modulator of multiple disease mechanisms rather than a single isolated pathway.  

Within this broader signaling framework, SMAD1 is important in the diabetes context because bone morphogenetic protein and mothers against decapentaplegic homolog signaling regulates vascular biology, tissue differentiation, and fibrotic remodeling. Diabetic complications, particularly nephropathy and vasculopathy, involve maladaptive transforming growth factor beta and bone morphogenetic protein pathway activity. Since SMAD1 is a core effector of bone morphogenetic protein signaling and is also linked in this list to GDF2 and bone morphogenetic protein nine-related endothelial regulation, it may represent a mechanistic bridge between developmental signaling and adult vascular homeostasis. Dysregulated SMAD1 activity could contribute to altered endothelial function, tissue repair responses, and fibrosis in diabetes-associated organ damage.[PubMed:11566864](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11566864) [PubMed:15329343](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15329343) [PubMed:21420501](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21420501) [PubMed:35594155](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35594155) [PubMed:34995814](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34995814)  

Another extracellular matrix-associated factor, SMOC2, is relevant to diabetes because extracellular matrix remodeling and angiogenesis are central to both chronic complications and tissue repair failure. In diabetic wounds and ischemic tissues, defective endothelial migration and abnormal matrix organization impair healing. Conversely, in the retina and kidney, excessive or maladaptive vascular responses can drive pathology. By promoting matrix assembly and endothelial proliferation and migration, SMOC2 may influence how diabetic tissues respond to injury and vascular stress. Its role is therefore most relevant to diabetic microvascular remodeling and wound healing biology.  

This emphasis on endothelial signaling is reinforced by another entry that appears to capture the core vascular endothelial growth factor signaling machinery central to diabetes complications, notwithstanding the probable naming inconsistency in the source annotation. Vascular endothelial growth factor pathway activation is one of the most important drivers of diabetic retinopathy, contributes to glomerular injury in diabetic nephropathy, and also influences wound healing and vascular permeability. The listed functions, including endothelial survival, migration, permeability control, and nitric oxide-related responses, map directly onto known mechanisms of diabetic microangiopathy. For this reason, this protein entry is among the most clinically relevant in the set, particularly for understanding retinal neovascularization, albuminuric kidney disease, and impaired vascular repair.  

Moving from signaling to matrix-associated restraint, ANGPTL7 is not a classic diabetes gene, but it is potentially relevant because extracellular matrix deposition and angiogenic restraint are recurring themes in diabetic complications. Matrix accumulation is central to diabetic fibrosis in organs such as the kidney, while dysregulated angiogenesis contributes to retinopathy and impaired tissue repair. The described role of ANGPTL7 in matrix deposition suggests a possible link to glucocorticoid-responsive remodeling processes, which may intersect with steroid-induced diabetes or with extracellular matrix changes under metabolic stress. Its anti-angiogenic function may also be informative in the broader context of diabetes-associated vascular imbalance.[PubMed:21199193](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21199193) [PubMed:25622036](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25622036)  

Consistent with that remodeling perspective, BMPER is potentially relevant to diabetes through its modulation of bone morphogenetic protein signaling, a pathway involved not only in skeletal biology but also in vascular homeostasis, adipose biology, and tissue remodeling. Although the annotation emphasizes osteoblasts and chondrocytes, bone morphogenetic protein pathway regulation can influence systemic metabolism and diabetic complication phenotypes, especially where calcification, fibrosis, or altered repair responses are present. Thus, BMPER may be a secondary but mechanistically plausible contributor to diabetes-related tissue remodeling.  

From tissue remodeling, the discussion naturally extends to cardiovascular adaptation, and HSPB6 is relevant to diabetes because cardiovascular dysfunction is a major cause of morbidity in diabetic patients. Its roles in vasorelaxation, cardiac contractility, cardioprotection, and post-injury angiogenesis suggest that it may modulate the response of the diabetic heart and vasculature to metabolic and oxidative stress. Since diabetes is associated with endothelial dysfunction, impaired vasodilation, and diabetic cardiomyopathy, a chaperone that supports vascular relaxation and tissue protection after injury could have substantial pathophysiological significance.  

A related matrix-centered consideration applies to HYAL1, which has a plausible connection to diabetes through extracellular matrix and hyaluronan turnover. Hyaluronan metabolism affects inflammation, fibrosis, vascular permeability, and wound repair, all of which are altered in diabetes. Although the annotation here is limited, enzymes that remodel hyaluronan can influence tissue stiffness, immune cell trafficking, and healing outcomes, suggesting potential relevance to diabetic nephropathy, skin ulcers, and adipose tissue inflammation.  

Finally, GRN may be relevant to diabetes through lysosomal function and proteostasis. Lysosomal dysfunction has emerged as an important feature of metabolic disease, influencing inflammation, lipid handling, autophagy, and beta-cell stress responses. By stabilizing cathepsin D, GRN could affect protein turnover and inflammatory signaling in metabolically active tissues. Although the diabetes connection is indirect based on the present annotation, GRN is noteworthy because disturbances in lysosomal biology contribute to insulin resistance and diabetic organ injury.

### Neutrophil degranulation (REAC:R-HSA-6798695) 

Neutrophil degranulation is a core effector program of innate immunity in which neutrophils release preformed antimicrobial and inflammatory mediators from intracellular granules into phagosomes or the extracellular space after activation. This process is tightly coordinated with neutrophil adhesion, migration, phagocytosis, oxidative burst, cytoskeletal remodeling, and, under some conditions, extracellular trap formation. The released cargo includes proteases, oxidant-generating enzymes, alarmins, matrix-remodeling proteins, and iron-binding proteins, such as myeloperoxidase, neutrophil elastase, matrix metalloproteinase eight, matrix metalloproteinase nine, lactoferrin, and other granule-associated molecules. Physiologically, degranulation contributes to rapid pathogen killing and orchestration of downstream immune responses. However, when excessive, chronic, spatially misdirected, or metabolically dysregulated, it can damage host tissues, amplify sterile inflammation, promote endothelial dysfunction, alter extracellular matrix turnover, and facilitate thrombosis. Because diabetes is characterized by hyperglycemia, altered cellular metabolism, oxidative stress, low-grade inflammation, vascular injury, and impaired host defense, neutrophil degranulation is highly relevant to disease initiation, progression, and complications. In this context, the pathway is perhaps best viewed as a double-edged process: it may be functionally defective in antimicrobial defense while simultaneously contributing to chronic inflammatory tissue injury in metabolic organs and the vasculature.  

Against this biological background, the collected literature indicates that neutrophil degranulation is closely linked to diabetes across both autoimmune and metabolic forms of the disease, as well as across several major complications. In type two diabetes, clinical evidence shows that circulating biomarkers of neutrophil degranulation, including myeloperoxidase, resistin, matrix metalloproteinase eight, and the matrix metalloproteinase nine and tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases one complex, are associated particularly with the restrictive echocardiographic pattern and diastolic dysfunction, supporting a role for neutrophil-derived inflammatory and matrix-remodeling mediators in diabetic cardiomyopathy and myocardial stiffness rather than merely reflecting generalized inflammation alone (PubMed:34129696). Mechanistically, hyperglycemia appears to reprogram neutrophil signaling and activation states: phosphoproteomic profiling demonstrated that high glucose activates distinct kinase networks linked to neutrophil functional responses, while homocysteine preferentially induced signaling associated with neutrophil degranulation and cytoskeletal remodeling, suggesting that the metabolic environment of diabetes directly shapes degranulation-related pathways and may bias neutrophils toward pathogenic inflammatory outputs (PubMed:35622142). At the same time, older functional work emphasized that diabetes can impair multiple neutrophil activities, including chemotaxis, phagocytosis, microbicidal capacity, migration, reactive oxygen species production, and cytokine release, indicating that diabetic neutrophils may exist in a paradoxical state in which host-defense functions are blunted whereas injurious inflammatory programs remain aberrantly activated or misdirected (PubMed:17665039). In type one diabetes, several studies support participation of neutrophil degranulation in autoimmune pathogenesis: review evidence indicates that neutrophil-derived cytotoxic granule products, reactive oxygen species, cytokines, and extracellular traps can injure pancreatic beta cells and amplify diabetogenic immune responses, while systems and transcriptomic studies further identify neutrophil degranulation among the immune pathways associated with type one diabetes biology and heterogeneity of beta-cell decline after diagnosis (PubMed:27181374, PubMed:37704687, PubMed:38961656). Beyond primary disease mechanisms, neutrophil degranulation also appears to contribute to diabetic complications. A recent review on extracellular traps in diabetes highlighted that neutrophil granule constituents such as myeloperoxidase and neutrophil elastase participate in inflammatory tissue injury, thrombosis, impaired wound healing, retinopathy, stroke, and coronary artery disease, linking degranulation to the broader spectrum of vascular and reparative dysfunction in diabetes (PubMed:36082273). Consistently, bioinformatic analysis of diabetes-related stroke identified granulin precursor as a hub gene connected to neutrophil extracellular trap formation through neutrophil degranulation, suggesting that this pathway may connect diabetes to heightened thromboinflammatory cerebrovascular risk (PubMed:38166912). Additional human studies reinforce the biomarker potential of this pathway, including elevated plasma lactoferrin, a neutrophil degranulation product, in type two diabetes with dry eye disease, where lactoferrin correlated with glycosylated hemoglobin, implying a relationship between glycemic burden and degranulation-associated inflammation (PubMed:40792303). Finally, intervention-related observations are compatible with a pathogenic role of neutrophil activation in metabolic disease, as lower neutrophil counts were associated with a greater likelihood of remission of type two diabetes during Mediterranean dietary intervention, indirectly supporting the concept that attenuation of neutrophil-driven inflammatory programs may accompany metabolic improvement (PubMed:40148287). Taken together, the available evidence supports neutrophil degranulation as a biologically plausible and clinically relevant pathway in diabetes, linking hyperglycemia and metabolic stress to innate immune dysregulation, pancreatic beta-cell injury, cardiovascular remodeling, thromboinflammation, mucosal and ocular inflammation, and impaired tissue repair.[PubMed:34129696](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34129696) [PubMed:35622142](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35622142) [PubMed:17665039](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17665039) [PubMed:27181374](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27181374) [PubMed:37704687](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37704687) [PubMed:38961656](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38961656) [PubMed:36082273](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36082273) [PubMed:38166912](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38166912) [PubMed:40792303](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40792303) [PubMed:40148287](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40148287) 

Building on this literature context, the enrichment results provide a quantitative view of how strongly this pathway may intersect with diabetes-related molecular changes. There were 88 diabetes-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of neutrophil degranulation, indicating substantial convergence of diabetes-related molecular signals on an innate immune effector program that links antimicrobial defense, inflammatory amplification, oxidative injury, extracellular matrix remodeling, endothelial dysfunction, and thrombotic susceptibility. This protein count of 88 supports a quantitatively robust enrichment signal and suggests that neutrophil granule release is not a peripheral event in diabetes biology, but rather a central process positioned at the interface of hyperglycemia, metabolic stress, vascular injury, and chronic low-grade inflammation. In the context of diabetes, the biological interpretation of this enrichment is especially important because neutrophil degranulation can exert both protective and pathogenic effects: on one hand, altered degranulation may impair pathogen clearance and contribute to defective host defense, while on the other hand, excessive or mislocalized release of proteases, oxidant-generating enzymes, alarmins, and matrix-remodeling proteins can intensify tissue damage in metabolic organs and the vasculature. The presence of 88 enriched proteins therefore argues for broad pathway involvement rather than isolated molecular participation, consistent with a systems-level perturbation of innate immune regulation in diabetes.

To complement this pathway-level interpretation, the network analysis below illustrates how these 88 proteins are connected at the protein-protein interaction level.

The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network of these 88 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for interactive inspection of the network topology and functional connectivity.

![PPI Network](imgs/446835cf-f984-43e5-b6fe-b685fd16e8f5.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=22FF4CD672AA9517)

With this network context in mind, the following section introduces several significant proteins identified during the function enrichment analysis and discusses their possible relevance to diabetes in a cautious and biologically grounded manner.

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  
ACAA1 is notable in the context of diabetes because altered lipid handling is a central feature of insulin resistance, hepatic steatosis, and lipotoxicity. By participating in peroxisomal beta-oxidation, ACAA1 contributes to the breakdown of very-long-chain and other fatty acyl-CoAs that cannot be managed efficiently by mitochondria alone. Impaired peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation can promote intracellular lipid accumulation and oxidative stress, both of which are mechanistically linked to reduced insulin responsiveness in liver and other metabolic tissues. Thus, ACAA1 stands out as a metabolically relevant protein whose function intersects directly with the dysregulated fatty acid flux that characterizes type 2 diabetes and related metabolic syndrome states.[PubMed:11734571](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11734571) [PubMed:2882519](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2882519)  

In a related metabolic-regulatory context, ADA2 points toward neuroendocrine control of glucose homeostasis. ADA2 is potentially relevant to diabetes because adrenergic signaling is an important regulator of glucose homeostasis, insulin secretion, and counter-regulatory stress responses. Inhibition of adenylate cyclase reduces cyclic adenosine monophosphate signaling, a pathway that strongly influences hormone secretion and metabolic adaptation. In pancreatic islets, alpha-2 adrenergic signaling is well known to suppress insulin release, and excessive sympathetic tone can therefore contribute to impaired glycemic control. Although the present annotation is concise, the receptor's core function places it within a biologically plausible axis linking neuroendocrine stress signaling to beta-cell dysfunction and hyperglycemia.  

Shifting from neuroendocrine regulation to innate immune signaling, BST2 may be relevant because diabetes is frequently accompanied by chronic inflammatory activation. BST2 is relevant to diabetes primarily through the intersection of innate immunity, chronic inflammation, and interferon signaling. Low-grade inflammatory activation is a hallmark of type 2 diabetes, while type 1 diabetes is strongly shaped by antiviral and interferon-related immune pathways. BST2 is particularly interesting because it is both an antiviral effector and an immunomodulatory molecule capable of influencing nuclear factor kappa B signaling and dendritic cell interferon responses. These properties make it a plausible contributor to inflammatory tissue stress, including in pancreatic islets or adipose tissue, where persistent innate immune activation can worsen insulin resistance or beta-cell injury. Its broad immune-regulatory profile therefore gives BST2 potential relevance to diabetes pathogenesis, especially in settings where viral triggers or interferon signatures are implicated.[PubMed:18200009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18200009) [PubMed:18342597](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18342597) [PubMed:19036818](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19036818) [PubMed:19879838](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19879838) [PubMed:20019814](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019814) [PubMed:20399176](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20399176) [PubMed:20419159](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20419159) [PubMed:20940320](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20940320) [PubMed:21529378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21529378) [PubMed:22520941](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22520941) [PubMed:19179289](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19179289) [PubMed:20686043](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20686043) [PubMed:20943977](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20943977) [PubMed:21621240](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21621240) [PubMed:26378163](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26378163) [PubMed:31199522](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31199522) [PubMed:22065321](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22065321) [PubMed:19564354](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19564354) [PubMed:26172439](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26172439) [PubMed:23028328](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23028328)  

Extending this theme of innate immune activation, CD14 may be one of the more direct links between inflammatory sensing and metabolic dysfunction. CD14 is one of the most compelling diabetes-related proteins in this list because it sits at the center of innate immune sensing and metabolic inflammation. Activation of the CD14-TLR4 axis by endotoxin or other inflammatory ligands promotes nuclear factor kappa B signaling and cytokine production, processes strongly implicated in insulin resistance, adipose tissue inflammation, and beta-cell stress. The relevance is particularly high for type 2 diabetes, where metabolic endotoxemia and chronic activation of innate immunity have been proposed to drive systemic insulin resistance. CD14 also binds electronegative low-density lipoprotein, linking inflammatory signaling with dyslipidemia, another major component of diabetic pathology. Overall, CD14 represents a mechanistic bridge between microbial products, sterile inflammation, lipid abnormalities, and impaired glucose metabolism.[PubMed:16148141](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16148141) [PubMed:15895089](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15895089) [PubMed:8612135](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8612135) [PubMed:19362712](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19362712)  

In parallel, CD300A may be relevant because inhibitory immune checkpoints can shape the amplitude of chronic metabolic inflammation. CD300A is relevant to diabetes because it functions as a brake on innate immune activation, especially on MYD88-dependent toll-like receptor signaling. Since chronic low-grade inflammation is a major driver of insulin resistance and tissue dysfunction in type 2 diabetes, inhibitory receptors such as CD300A may influence the threshold and duration of inflammatory responses in metabolic tissues. By restraining toll-like receptor signaling, CD300A could theoretically mitigate cytokine production and immune-mediated damage. This is particularly important because excessive innate immune activation in adipose tissue, liver, and pancreatic islets contributes to metabolic deterioration. Therefore, CD300A stands out as a potential endogenous counter-regulatory factor in diabetes-associated inflammation.[PubMed:12874256](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12874256) [PubMed:12893283](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12893283) [PubMed:16339535](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16339535)  

Moving from inflammatory control to tissue remodeling and survival signaling, CHI3L1 may also have potential relevance. CHI3L1 is highly relevant to diabetes because it combines inflammatory, remodeling, and survival-related functions that map closely onto diabetic complications and metabolic tissue dysfunction. Its ability to regulate macrophage differentiation, dendritic cell accumulation, and inflammatory cytokine pathways suggests a role in the chronic immune activation observed in obesity and type 2 diabetes. Moreover, its involvement in AKT1 signaling is particularly notable, as AKT is a central node in insulin signaling and cellular survival pathways. CHI3L1 may therefore influence both inflammatory tone and tissue adaptation in organs commonly affected by diabetes, including adipose tissue, vasculature, gut, and lung.
