This makes it a strong candidate for relevance not only to metabolic dysregulation but also to fibrosis, repair, and chronic complications.  

A more indirect but still potentially meaningful connection to diabetic tissue stress may be seen with CKAP4. CKAP4 has a more indirect but still potentially meaningful connection to diabetes through regulation of cell growth and stress signaling. Diabetes is associated with altered epithelial integrity, impaired repair responses, and abnormal proliferative control in several tissues, including kidney and vasculature. A receptor that mediates antiproliferative signaling could therefore influence tissue remodeling or regenerative capacity under diabetic stress. Although the current annotation does not directly place CKAP4 in a metabolic pathway, its role in cell-surface signaling and proliferation control may be relevant in the context of diabetic complications characterized by epithelial dysfunction.  

Continuing toward proteins that may amplify inflammatory effector damage, CTSC is of particular interest. CTSC is of interest for diabetes because it amplifies protease networks involved in inflammation and immune-cell effector function. By activating elastase, cathepsin G, and granzymes, CTSC can contribute to tissue injury, extracellular matrix remodeling, and immune-mediated cytotoxicity. These processes are relevant to diabetic inflammation, vascular injury, and potentially beta-cell damage in autoimmune contexts. In type 2 diabetes, neutrophil and myeloid protease activity has been linked to chronic inflammatory tissue remodeling, whereas in type 1 diabetes, granzyme-related pathways may influence immune destruction of beta cells. CTSC therefore represents a plausible upstream regulator of damaging proteolytic cascades in diabetes-associated pathology.[PubMed:1586157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1586157) [PubMed:8428921](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8428921)  

At the level of intracellular proteostasis, ERP44 may be relevant because beta-cell function depends heavily on endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis. ERP44 is particularly relevant to diabetes because endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative protein folding, and calcium homeostasis are all central determinants of beta-cell health and insulin secretory capacity. Pancreatic beta cells are highly dependent on efficient endoplasmic reticulum function to fold and process insulin, and disturbances in endoplasmic reticulum redox balance can trigger the unfolded protein response and apoptosis. ERP44 also regulates ITPR1-mediated calcium flux, a key factor in stimulus-secretion coupling and cell survival. For these reasons, ERP44 stands out as a strong mechanistic candidate linking proteostasis stress to beta-cell dysfunction and progressive diabetes.[PubMed:11847130](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11847130) [PubMed:14517240](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14517240) [PubMed:15652484](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15652484) [PubMed:29858230](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29858230)  

Within this same metabolic-stress framework, FGR appears especially notable because its annotated functions intersect directly with insulin action. FGR is one of the strongest diabetes-relevant proteins in this dataset because its annotated functions directly involve insulin action, glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, and hepatic endoplasmic reticulum stress adaptation. These are core biological processes disrupted in type 2 diabetes. The annotation explicitly states that FGR is necessary for insulin-stimulated increases in glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis, indicating a direct role in insulin sensitivity. In addition, its promotion of XBP1 nuclear translocation during metabolic overloading suggests that FGR may help coordinate adaptive unfolded protein response signaling in the liver, thereby influencing glucose tolerance. This combination of insulin signaling and endoplasmic reticulum stress regulation makes FGR especially important for understanding mechanisms of metabolic dysfunction.[PubMed:17626883](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17626883) [PubMed:19805105](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19805105) [PubMed:7518429](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7518429) [PubMed:20348923](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20348923)  

A more indirect metabolic contribution may be considered for GGH through one-carbon metabolism and vascular biology. GGH may be relevant to diabetes through one-carbon metabolism, folate handling, and downstream effects on vascular health. Folate metabolism influences methylation pathways, homocysteine balance, and cellular proliferation, all of which can shape cardiometabolic risk and diabetic complications. Although GGH is not a canonical diabetes gene, altered folate metabolism may affect endothelial function and inflammation, potentially modifying susceptibility to microvascular and macrovascular disease in diabetes. Its role is therefore likely indirect but biologically plausible, especially in relation to complication risk.[PubMed:11005824](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11005824) [PubMed:8816764](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8816764)  

By contrast, GPI has a more central relationship to glucose handling itself. GPI is highly relevant to diabetes because it occupies a central position in glucose metabolism. As a glycolytic enzyme, it contributes directly to intracellular glucose utilization, and disturbances in glycolytic flux are fundamental to both insulin resistance and beta-cell dysfunction. Its extracellular cytokine-like functions further broaden its significance, suggesting additional roles in angiogenesis, immune signaling, and tissue adaptation. These noncanonical functions are especially interesting in diabetes, a disease characterized not only by disordered glucose metabolism but also by vascular remodeling and chronic inflammation. GPI therefore stands out as a multifunctional protein linking core carbohydrate metabolism with systemic disease processes.[PubMed:28803808](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28803808) [PubMed:11437381](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11437381) [PubMed:11004567](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11004567) [PubMed:3352745](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3352745)  

Returning to immune restraint, LAIR1 may be relevant as a broad suppressor of inflammatory signaling. LAIR1 is important in diabetes because it is a broad negative regulator of immune activation, cytokine production, and nuclear factor kappa B signaling. These features are highly relevant to both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. In type 1 diabetes, inhibitory receptors that constrain lymphocyte activation may influence autoimmune beta-cell destruction. In type 2 diabetes, suppression of inflammatory cytokines and nuclear factor kappa B activity may help limit the chronic innate and adaptive immune activation that contributes to insulin resistance. LAIR1 therefore stands out as a potentially protective immunoregulatory node whose reduced activity could favor persistent inflammation and tissue damage.  

At the level of intermediary metabolism, NIT2 may have a subtler but still plausible connection to diabetes-related metabolic flexibility. NIT2 is relevant to diabetes because it participates in intermediary metabolism and detoxification of potentially harmful nitrogen-containing metabolites. Its products, 2-oxoglutarate and oxaloacetate, are central metabolites in the tricarboxylic acid cycle and gluconeogenic pathways. Maintenance of these metabolic nodes is important in tissues with high energetic demand, including liver and pancreatic islets. While the connection to diabetes is less direct than for insulin signaling proteins, NIT2 may influence metabolic flexibility and cellular stress tolerance, both of which are impaired in diabetes.[PubMed:19596042](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19596042) [PubMed:28373563](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28373563)  

Lipid trafficking provides another important layer of diabetes biology, and NPC2 may be relevant within this context. NPC2 is highly pertinent to diabetes because cholesterol trafficking and lysosomal lipid handling are increasingly recognized as major determinants of insulin sensitivity, inflammation, and beta-cell function. Defective intracellular cholesterol export can promote lipotoxic stress, organelle dysfunction, and inflammatory activation. In pancreatic beta cells, excessive cholesterol accumulation impairs insulin secretion, while in macrophages and liver it contributes to metabolic inflammation and steatosis. NPC2 therefore stands out as a lipid-homeostasis factor with plausible relevance to multiple aspects of diabetes pathogenesis, including dyslipidemia and organelle stress.[PubMed:12591949](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12591949) [PubMed:17018531](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17018531) [PubMed:21315718](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21315718) [PubMed:26296895](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26296895)  

Shifting from intracellular lipid handling to vascular integrity, PTPRB may be relevant because endothelial dysfunction is a major feature of diabetic complications. PTPRB is relevant to diabetes chiefly because endothelial dysfunction is a defining feature of diabetic vascular disease. Maintenance of endothelial junction integrity, polarity, and vascular lumen architecture is essential for barrier function and microvascular health. In diabetes, chronic hyperglycemia, oxidative stress, and inflammation disrupt endothelial cohesion, thereby contributing to nephropathy, retinopathy, and cardiovascular complications. A protein that stabilizes endothelial organization may therefore be highly important in modulating susceptibility to diabetic microangiopathy and vascular leak.[PubMed:20332120](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20332120) [PubMed:9220534](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9220534) [PubMed:24806444](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24806444) [PubMed:27466317](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27466317) [PubMed:33972531](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33972531)  

Extracellular matrix remodeling represents another major component of chronic diabetic injury, which brings QSOX1 into consideration. QSOX1 is potentially important in diabetes because extracellular matrix remodeling and fibrosis are major components of diabetic complications. By promoting disulfide bond formation in extracellular proteins and supporting laminin incorporation into matrix, QSOX1 can influence tissue architecture, adhesion, and wound repair. These functions are especially relevant in diabetes, where impaired matrix organization contributes to poor wound healing, vascular basement membrane abnormalities, and fibrotic remodeling in organs such as kidney and heart. QSOX1 therefore stands out as a plausible contributor to structural tissue changes associated with chronic hyperglycemia.[PubMed:17331072](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17331072) [PubMed:18393449](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18393449) [PubMed:23704371](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23704371) [PubMed:23867277](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23867277) [PubMed:30367560](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30367560) [PubMed:22801504](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22801504)  

At the interface of innate immunity and mitochondrial biology, RNASET2 may also warrant attention. RNASET2 is relevant to diabetes because it links innate immune activation with mitochondrial ribonucleic acid homeostasis. The innate immune system has a major role in both autoimmune and metabolic forms of diabetes, and nucleic acid sensing pathways can drive inflammatory cytokine production. In addition, mitochondrial dysfunction is a key feature of insulin resistance and beta-cell failure. By participating in both ribonucleic acid sensing-related immunity and mitochondrial ribonucleic acid turnover, RNASET2 occupies an interesting intersection between inflammation and cellular energetics. This dual role makes it a plausible modifier of diabetes susceptibility or progression, particularly where sterile inflammation and mitochondrial stress coexist.[PubMed:31778653](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31778653) [PubMed:38697119](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38697119) [PubMed:28730546](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28730546) [PubMed:30184494](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184494) [PubMed:30385512](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30385512)  

Another possible inflammatory link is provided by S100P through receptor for advanced glycation end products signaling. S100P is notable in diabetes because receptor for advanced glycation end products signaling is a well-established pathogenic pathway in hyperglycemia, advanced glycation end product biology, inflammation, and vascular damage. A protein capable of stimulating proliferation through receptor for advanced glycation end products may amplify inflammatory and remodeling responses in diabetic tissues. Its calcium-sensing properties are also relevant, given the importance of calcium signaling in insulin secretion and epithelial function. Thus, S100P may connect calcium-dependent signaling with receptor for advanced glycation end products-mediated inflammatory pathways that are central to diabetic complications, especially vascular and epithelial injury.  

Within the secretory pathway, SRP14 may be relevant because insulin biosynthesis depends on efficient protein targeting to the endoplasmic reticulum. SRP14 may be relevant to diabetes because efficient targeting of secretory proteins to the endoplasmic reticulum is essential for insulin biosynthesis and processing. Pancreatic beta cells are among the most secretory cell types in the body and are highly sensitive to defects in endoplasmic reticulum protein handling. Although SRP14 is a general secretory pathway component rather than a diabetes-specific factor, disruption of cotranslational targeting could aggravate endoplasmic reticulum stress and impair insulin production. Its significance therefore lies in the broader framework of beta-cell proteostasis.[PubMed:11089964](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11089964)  

Closely related to this theme, TXNDC5 may be especially important because insulin maturation depends on correct disulfide bond formation. TXNDC5 is strongly relevant to diabetes because it directly participates in endoplasmic reticulum protein folding and has documented activity toward insulin disulfide bonds. Proper disulfide bond formation is indispensable for insulin maturation, and endoplasmic reticulum oxidative folding defects are a major cause of beta-cell stress and failure. Given the extraordinary secretory burden placed on beta cells, proteins such as TXNDC5 may critically influence insulin biosynthesis, proinsulin processing quality, and susceptibility to unfolded protein response activation. This makes TXNDC5 a particularly compelling candidate in mechanisms linking endoplasmic reticulum dysfunction to diabetes.[PubMed:12930873](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12930873) [PubMed:14971039](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14971039)  

Mitochondrial dynamics and tissue repair add another dimension to diabetes complications, which may make VAT1 of interest. VAT1 is potentially relevant to diabetes through two disease-relevant processes: mitochondrial dynamics and wound repair. Mitochondrial fusion-fission balance is critical for insulin sensitivity, beta-cell function, and cellular stress adaptation, while impaired epidermal repair is a hallmark of diabetes-associated chronic wounds. Because VAT1 negatively regulates mitochondrial fusion and participates in calcium-regulated repair responses, it may influence both metabolic resilience and tissue healing. This makes it an interesting, though less established, candidate in the biology of diabetic complications.  

Finally, VNN1 may be relevant in the broader setting of redox balance and energy metabolism. VNN1 is relevant to diabetes because it influences coenzyme A precursor metabolism and generates cysteamine, a small thiol that can affect redox balance and inflammatory responses. Pantothenic acid recycling is tied to lipid and energy metabolism, while redox-active metabolites are important in oxidative stress, a major contributor to insulin resistance and diabetic tissue injury. Although the annotation is brief, VNN1's metabolic and redox-related functions make it a plausible participant in pathways that influence glucose-lipid homeostasis and chronic inflammation.
